findings.claim: Hanus et al. 2011 fitted each per-observatory sparse lightcurve from AstDyS with a phase curve and rejected any observatory whose median or 'FWHM' residual was about 0.2 mag or more. Their Table 1 residual medians: 689 0.15, 703 0.19, E12 0.15, G96 0.17, 950 0.15, 699 0.18, Hipparcos 0.11. Rejected: 691 0.24, 704 0.42, 608 0.27, 644 0.24, 683 0.20, H07 0.23.
findings.quote: Observatories with a high median or "FWHM" value (≳0.2 mag for both) are not suitable for the lightcurve inversion

findings.claim: Hanus et al. 2011 weighted each observatory relative to dense lightcurves, which had weight 1 and an assumed accuracy of about 0.02 mag. Weights: 689 USNO 0.3, Hipparcos 0.3, 703 CSS 0.15, 950 La Palma 0.15, 699 LONEOS 0.1, E12 Siding Spring 0.1, G96 Mt Lemmon 0.1. All other observatories, including 691, 704, 608 and 644, got weight 0.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134; arXiv:1104.4114
findings.quote: relative to dense data, which has a unity weight (see Table 1). We assumed that the typical accuracy of dense lightcurves is ∼0.02 mag.

findings.claim: Sparse data are kept as one 'sparse lightcurve' per observatory per asteroid. Hanus 2011 required at least 30 points, computed the geometry, corrected for light-time and reduced brightness to 1 AU (i.e. calibrated data). A typical asteroid had 2-4 such lightcurves covering about 10-15 years.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134; arXiv:1104.4114
findings.quote: For any given asteroid, we have typically 2–4 sparse lightcurves from different observatories covering the last ∼10–15 years.

findings.claim: To estimate each observatory's quality, Hanus 2011 fitted every sparse lightcurve with f(alpha) = cos^2(alpha/2) [a exp(-alpha/b) + c alpha + d], with a, b, c, d free, and built histograms of the rms residuals per observatory.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134; arXiv:1104.4114
findings.quote: we assumed that the brightness vs. solar phase angle relation can be fitted with a simple relation for each sparse lightcurve

findings.claim: Most survey photometry in AstDyS/MPC is quantized to 0.1 mag. Hanus 2011 notes the mean lightcurve amplitude is about 0.3 mag and 19% of asteroids have amplitude of 0.5 mag or more, so 0.1-mag data can still constrain spin and shape for many objects. The USNO (689) data used by Durech et al. 2009 had about 8-10% uncertainty.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134; arXiv:1104.4114
findings.quote: In most cases, asteroid magnitudes are given to only one decimal place, i.e., the accuracy is 0.1 mag at best.

findings.claim: Hanus 2011 (and Hanus & Durech 2012) defined a unique solution as follows. (i) The best period has at least 10% lower chi2 than all other periods. (ii) Only one pole has at least 10% lower chi2 than the others, apart from the lambda+-180 deg mirror. (iii) The solution passes the additional tests.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134; arXiv:1104.4114
findings.quote: there is only one pole solution with at least 10% lower χ2 than the others (with a possible ambiguity for λ ± 180°)

findings.claim: Hanus 2011 scan windows: centred on the LCDB period with half-width +-1%, +-5% or +-20% of P for reliability codes 4, 3 and 2; half and double periods were tested afterwards. Without a prior period they scanned 2-30 h.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134; arXiv:1104.4114
findings.quote: a range of ±1%, ±5% and ±20% of P for reliability codes 4, 3 and 2, respectively

findings.claim: Hanus 2011 additional tests: (1) reject a model if the spin axis is more than 30 deg from the maximum-inertia axis, with an exception for some elongated shapes; (2) reject if a fit at 2P or P/2 has chi2 below 1.1 chi2(P); (3) for sparse-only models, rerun with 90% of the points; (4) compare with existing DAMIT models; (5) invert 10 'mock' objects.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134; arXiv:1104.4114
findings.quote: if the χ2 was lower than 1.1χ2 of the solution with period P, we rejected the model as unreliable

findings.claim: Hanus 2011 inverted about 2300 data sets (about 900 sparse-only) and obtained 80 new unique models (16 from sparse data alone) plus 30 partial models (mean beta reported when the beta dispersion was below 50 deg). All 16 sparse-only models of asteroids already in DAMIT were similar to the DAMIT models. Mock tests gave pole uncertainty of about +-10 deg and period uncertainty of about 0.1 of the spacing between local minima.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134; arXiv:1104.4114
findings.quote: The typical uncertainty in pole direction was ±10° and, for the period, ∼0.1 times the difference between the two local minimums

findings.claim: Catalina (703) sparse data alone, typical accuracy about 12%: of 185 asteroids with at least 50 CSS points and an existing model, 13 gave a 'unique' solution, but only 7 of those agreed with the independent model. Six were formally unique but had the wrong period.
findings.source: Hanus & Durech 2012, Planet. Space Sci. 73, 75; arXiv:1301.7205
findings.quote: In 13 cases, we were able to derive their unique solutions. Only in 7 cases the solution was in an agreement with the model

findings.claim: Hanus & Durech 2012 used period step Pstep = 0.8 DeltaP with DeltaP = P^2/T. After testing shape resolutions n = 2-6 and steps 0.8 and 0.5 DeltaP, they recommend n = 6 with Pstep = 0.5 DeltaP and, if a unique solution appears, a rerun with n = 3 and 0.5 DeltaP. Wrong 'unique' solutions never appeared for n = 2 or 3.
findings.source: Hanus & Durech 2012, Planet. Space Sci. 73, 75; arXiv:1301.7205
findings.quote: we should use the values n = 6 and Pstep = 0.5∆P for resolution and period step, respectively

findings.claim: For correct CSS-only solutions, the period dispersion across resolutions was below DeltaP (about 1e-3 h for P = 10 h over a 10-year span). Pole latitude scattered by about 20 deg or less, while pole longitude often scattered by 50 deg or more.
findings.source: Hanus & Durech 2012, Planet. Space Sci. 73, 75; arXiv:1301.7205
findings.quote: The dispersion in the ecliptic latitude of the pole direction was usually ≲20°, but in the ecliptic longitude of the pole direction often ≳50°.

findings.claim: Hanus et al. 2013 used sparse data from 689, 703 and 950 with a priori LCDB periods, or 2-100 h when the period was unknown. Sparse-only solutions had to be stable at both n = 3 and n = 6, the typical n being 6, i.e. 49 shape parameters. Results: 119 combined models and 20 CSS-only models. Quoted pole uncertainty is 10-20 deg for combined models and 20-40 deg for CSS-only models.
findings.quote: The correct solution had to be stable for both low (n = 3) and high (n = 6) shape resolutions.

findings.claim: Hanus et al. 2016 weights relative to dense data (weight 1): USNO 689 = 0.3, CSS 703 = 0.15, and 0.1 for the whole Lowell re-calibrated set. They note that one weight for a mix of observatories over- or under-weights individual asteroids. 57 of their 250 models were from USNO+CSS sparse data alone, with 2-1000 h typically scanned.
findings.quote: weighting them with respect to dense data (unity weight) by 0.3 and 0.15, respectively

findings.claim: Hanus 2016 typical pole uncertainties: 5 deg or less for large multi-apparition dense data sets; 5-10 deg for dense plus sparse; 10-30 deg in beta (10-30 deg / cos beta in lambda) for few-apparition dense plus sparse, or sparse alone. Sparse-based shapes have many flat facets and sharp edges.
findings.quote: ∼10−30° in β and ∼10−30°/cos β in λ for models based on combined few-apparition dense data with sparse-in-time measurements or only sparse-in-time data

findings.claim: Durech et al. 2016 (Lowell database, 0.10-0.20 mag accuracy, about 480 points per asteroid for numbers below 10,000) scanned 2-100 h with 10 isotropic initial poles per trial period. That is 200,000-300,000 trial periods per asteroid (about a month on one CPU), run on Asteroids@home. With an LCDB prior: P +-5% for U = 3/3-, +-10% for U = 2+.
findings.quote: For each trial period, we started with ten initial pole directions that were isotropically distributed on a sphere.

findings.claim: Durech 2016 Test 1: the global minimum must be at least 5% lower than every chi2 outside Pmin +- 0.5 Pmin^2/DeltaT. The 5% level was tuned against DAMIT to give about 1% false positives. Test 2: the periods from n = 3 and n = 6 must agree. Test 3: without an LCDB prior, only Pmin < 20 h is accepted.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2016, A&A 587, A48; arXiv:1601.02909
findings.quote: lowest χ2 corresponding to the rotation period Pmin is at least 5% lower than all other χ2 values for periods outside the Pmin ±0.5P²min/∆T interval

findings.claim: Durech 2016 pole and shape tests: at most two distinct poles (more than 30 deg apart) at least 5% deeper than the others; for a pair, |beta1 - beta2| < 50 deg and mod(|lambda1 - lambda2|, 180 deg) > 120 deg; moment of inertia about the principal axis over that about the rotation axis < 1.1; a bootstrap rerun must recover the same Pmin; then visual inspection.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2016, A&A 587, A48; arXiv:1601.02909
findings.quote: The ratio of the moment of inertia along the principal axis to that along the actual rotation axis should be less than 1.1.

findings.claim: Durech 2016 results: Lowell data for the first 100,000 numbered asteroids gave about 600 models passing all tests, 328 of them new. Of 279 that overlap DAMIT, 275 had the same period and pole differences below 50 deg (mean 15 deg, median 13 deg). False positives were about a few percent, and models are biased toward elongated, high-amplitude bodies.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2016, A&A 587, A48; arXiv:1601.02909
findings.quote: the mean value is 15° and the median 13°, which can be interpreted as a typical error in the pole determination

findings.claim: Durech 2016 also searched periods with a triaxial ellipsoid under geometric scattering, which is analytic and always rotates about its maximum-inertia axis, and then used that period to start convex inversion. Where convex models gave many equally good periods, the ellipsoid often gave a unique and correct one.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2016, A&A 587, A48; arXiv:1601.02909
findings.quote: The accuracy of this simplified model is sufficient to reveal the correct rotation period as a significant minimum of χ2

findings.claim: Durech et al. 2018 (Lowell + WISE) replaced the fixed 5% with a per-asteroid threshold chi2_tr = (1 + 0.5 sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min. nu = Ndata - Nparams, with Nparams = 3 spin + 3 phase-function + (n+1)^2 shape parameters (or 2 for an ellipsoid). The old 5% level corresponds to nu = 200.
findings.source: Durech, Hanus & Ali-Lagoa 2018, A&A 617, A57; arXiv:1807.02083
findings.quote: we computed the acceptance level for each asteroid individually according to the formula χ2tr = (1 + 0.5 √2/ν) χ2min

findings.claim: Durech 2018 pipeline: scan 2-100 h independently with convex n = 3, convex n = 6 and ellipsoids. The unique periods from n = 3 and n = 6 must agree. If Pmin > 50 h, also scan 100-1000 h. More than two poles under chi2_tr gives a partial model, reported if the beta values span 50 deg or less (Delta <= 25 deg). Two poles must differ by less than 50 deg in beta and 120-240 deg in lambda. Then an inertia check and a visual check.
findings.source: Durech, Hanus & Ali-Lagoa 2018, A&A 617, A57; arXiv:1807.02083
findings.quote: the difference in β had to be smaller than 50° and the difference in λ 120–240°

findings.claim: Durech 2018: ellipsoid period search is about 100 times faster and more efficient than convex search, because flexible convex models can fit a wrong period with a non-physical shape. Of the 662 new models, 169 came from convex period search, 513 from ellipsoids and 20 from both. After the period is found, the pole search is done with convex shapes.
findings.source: Durech, Hanus & Ali-Lagoa 2018, A&A 617, A57; arXiv:1807.02083
findings.quote: ellipsoidal models are more efficient in finding the correct rotation period because convex models can formally fit the data with an incorrect period

findings.claim: Durech 2018 results: about 75,000 asteroids gave 908 unique models (about 1.2%) plus 789 partial models. Of 246 already in DAMIT, 237 had the correct period, with mean pole difference 12 deg and median 9 deg. The convex models were slightly less elongated than DAMIT ones (mean a/b and b/c ratios DAMIT/ours about 1.06).
findings.source: Durech, Hanus & Ali-Lagoa 2018, A&A 617, A57; arXiv:1807.02083
findings.quote: The mean pole difference was 12° and the median value was 9°.

findings.claim: Gaia DR2 inversion used chi2_tr = (1 + sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min, i.e. factor 1 instead of 1/2. Parameters: p = 6 for the ellipsoid (P, lambda, beta, a linear phase slope, a/c, b/c) and p = 20 for a convex n = 3 model. Only the linear phase term was fitted because Gaia phase angles are above 10 deg. Periodograms were rejected unless every RMS exceeded 0.005 mag and only one period had RMS below 0.01.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91; arXiv:1810.04485
findings.quote: we only selected periodograms with all RMS values > 0.005 mag. Another requirement was that there should be only one period with RMS below 0.01.

findings.claim: Durech & Hanus 2018 gave all Gaia DR2 points equal weight and ignored the individual errors, since model errors exceed the 1-2% photometric errors. They report that ground-based sparse surveys give robust models for less than 1% of asteroids.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91; arXiv:1810.04485
findings.quote: All data points were given the same weight; we did not take into account errors of individual measurements.

findings.claim: Gaia DR2 (10-50 points per asteroid): correct-period fraction exceeds 0.5 only when N > 30. 173 models were derived, 44 of them already in DAMIT, with mean pole difference 20 deg and 7 outliers above 60 deg (mostly neighbouring local minima in period). n = 3 convex shapes are unrealistic, with sharp edges.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91; arXiv:1810.04485
findings.quote: For N > 30, the solution of the inverse problem is often successful and the parameters are likely to be correct in most cases.

findings.claim: Durech et al. 2019 joint Gaia DR2 + Lowell fit: chi2_rel = sum over Gaia residuals^2 + w * sum over Lowell residuals^2, with w = 0.01 (0.1-mag versus 0.01-mag errors); w = 0.05 and 0.1 were also tested. Threshold chi2_tr = (1 + k sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min with k = 1, 1/2, 1/3. For w = 0.01, convex models gave 287, 522, 641 unique periods with 87%, 86%, 83% correct against LCDB (within 10%); ellipsoids gave 710, 997, 1215 with 90%, 85%, 78%.
findings.source: Durech, Hanus & Vanco 2019, A&A 631, A2; arXiv:1909.09395
findings.quote: the weight of Lowell data with respect to Gaia should be w = 0.01

findings.claim: Durech 2019 states the adopted values as w = 0.01, 'k = 3' for convex models and k = 1 for ellipsoids. Since only k = 1, 1/2 and 1/3 were tested, 'k = 3' is probably a typo for 1/3. About 15% of the accepted periods were wrong, but most of these failed later checks. 1142 models passed all checks; of 367 in DAMIT, 4 had completely different periods and 11 sat in a neighbouring local minimum with poles more than 60 deg off.
findings.source: Durech, Hanus & Vanco 2019, A&A 631, A2; arXiv:1909.09395
findings.quote: For the final analysis, we adopted values w = 0.01, k = 3 for convex models and k = 1 for ellipsoids.

findings.claim: For ATLAS, Durech et al. 2020 fitted a linear-exponential phase function, as in Hanus 2011, and clipped points deviating by more than 2.5 rms, which removed about 15% of points. They kept asteroids with at least 100 observations (about 98,000).
findings.source: Durech et al. 2020, A&A 643, A59; arXiv:2010.01820
findings.quote: we set up this limit to 2.5 rms, which seemed to be a good compromise that removed most of the outliers

findings.claim: ATLAS 2015-2018 data: periods 2-1000 h were scanned with both convex and ellipsoid models. Only about 5000 of about 100,000 asteroids gave a reliable sidereal period on the full interval. With an LCDB prior the window was +-5% (U = 3/3-), +-10% (U = 2+) or +-20% (U = 2).
findings.source: Durech et al. 2020, A&A 643, A59; arXiv:2010.01820
findings.quote: limited our search intervals to ±5% around PLCDB for U = 3 or 3−, to ±10% for U = 2+, and to ±20% for U = 2

findings.claim: Scattering law used in the ATLAS work: S = f(alpha) mu mu0 [1/(mu + mu0) + c] with c = 0.1 fixed, and f(alpha) = A0 exp(-alpha/D) + k alpha + 1 with A0, D, k optimized and k constrained non-positive. The two filters (c, o) share one phase function, and the c-o colour is fitted as a free scale factor between the per-filter data sets.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2020, A&A 643, A59; arXiv:2010.01820
findings.quote: was modeled as a free scale factor between the data sets in two filters, or equivalently as an offset in magnitude scale

findings.claim: ATLAS results: about 2750 unique models (950 already known; 1800 new, of which 705 full, 191 full with an LCDB prior, 671 partial, 225 partial with a prior), i.e. under 3% of about 100,000. Errors came from 100 bootstrap resamplings. Mean rms residual was 0.08 mag for P < 20 h and 0.12 mag for P > 100 h.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2020, A&A 643, A59; arXiv:2010.01820
findings.quote: the success rate of unique model determination from the current data set is not very high (less than 3000 models from about 100,000 asteroids)

findings.claim: Gaia DR3: 2-10,000 h scanned with step 0.8 DeltaP for convex models and 0.5 DeltaP for ellipsoids, where DeltaP = 0.5 P^2/T (uniform in frequency, step 0.4/T). Convex shape n = 3 (288 facets, 15 free coefficients). Minimum relative error 0.01. Only the phase slope k was fitted; a0 = 0.5, d = 0.1 and c = 0.1 were fixed. Sample: asteroids with at least 21 points.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24; arXiv:2305.10798
findings.quote: The step size in the period was set to 0.8 ∆P, where ∆P = 0.5 P2/T is a typical distance between local minima in the period

findings.claim: Gaia DR3 period uniqueness: every other period must have chi2 > (1 + sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min, and every local minimum must have RMS > 0.01. Convex funnel: 14,192 unique periods, then 11,854 with 1-2 poles, 8820 with inertia ratio < 1.1, and 8230 with |dbeta| <= 50 deg and dlambda >= 120 deg. Ellipsoid funnel: 16,010, then 9910, 7873, 7122.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24; arXiv:2305.10798
findings.quote: the root mean square (RMS) residuals of all local minima had to be higher than 0.01

findings.claim: Gaia DR3 stability test: 10 jackknife runs, each removing 10% of the points, and at least 9 of 10 must return the original period within 0.1%. Final 8596 models. The false-solution rate against LCDB U = 3 periods was about 0.6% (5 of 848). Success rate rises from a few percent at N = 21 to about 40% at N around 60.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24; arXiv:2305.10798
findings.quote: selected only asteroids for which all ten jackknife periods were the same (within 0.1%) as the original period

findings.claim: Durech & Hanus 2023 list the ellipsoid's advantages: fewer parameters, physically correct rotation, no false half-period solutions, about 100 times faster. Its limit is lightcurves that are not simple double sinusoids. Of 1324 DR3 models also in DAMIT, 33 periods disagreed, and in most of those the DAMIT model, often built from Lowell sparse data alone, was the wrong one.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24; arXiv:2305.10798
findings.quote: However, ellipsoidal shape models are insufficient when an asteroid's light curve significantly differs from a simple double sinusoidal curve.

findings.claim: ASAS-SN V-band, Hanus et al. 2021: 2-1500 h scanned in steps of 0.5 DeltaP, with DeltaP/P = 0.5 P/T, and 10 isotropic initial poles. At least 60 points were required, since the model has 55 parameters (49 shape at n = 6, 3 spin, 3 phase). Threshold chi2_tr = (1 + p sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min, with p = 0.5 for convex and p = 0.6 for ellipsoids chosen against LCDB (about 3% inconsistent).
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2021, A&A 654, A48; arXiv:2107.10027
findings.quote: So we select p = 0.5 as an optimal value in the CI and p = 0.6 in the tri-axial ellipsoid shape analyses.

findings.claim: ASAS-SN preprocessing: drop points more than 0.7 mag from the predicted magnitude; fit the phase function and clip at 2.5 sigma (linear part only if 30 or fewer points or no low-phase data); keep only points with errors below 0.15 mag (about 30% removed). Result: 760 unique models from 5283 asteroids (about 15%, versus about 3% for ATLAS/Gaia DR2 and 1% or less for Lowell). Poles rarely differ from DAMIT by more than 30 deg.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2021, A&A 654, A48; arXiv:2107.10027
findings.quote: we derived unique spin state and shape solutions for 760 asteroids. This corresponds to a success rate of about 15%

findings.claim: The Asteroids IV review states the basic principle: an internally calibrated sparse data set is treated as one very long, sparsely sampled lightcurve. Current surveys reach accuracy scarcely better than 0.1 mag, and for noisy or limited sparse data a triaxial ellipsoid is usually enough to find the period and spin.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2015, in Asteroids IV, p. 183; arXiv:1502.04816
findings.quote: Provided the whole sparse data set is internally calibrated, it can be used the same way as a standard lightcurve

findings.claim: DAMIT convexinv input format: each lightcurve block starts with the number of points and a flag, 0 = relative or 1 = calibrated. Calibrated brightness is in intensity units reduced to unit distances. Recommended settings: l = m = 6, 8-10 triangulation rows (8n^2 facets), and phase function starting values a = 0.5, d = 0.1, k = -0.5, c = 0.1. The manual warns that fitting phase parameters with only relative data diverges.
findings.source: DAMIT convexinv manual (convexinv_doc.pdf, v0.2.1, Kaasalainen/Durech)
findings.quote: Each lightcurve starts with the number of points and 0/1 code for a relative (0) or calibrated (1) lightcurve.

findings.claim: DAMIT manual: keep the dark facet below 1% of the total area by increasing the convexity regularization (typical 0.1, possibly orders of magnitude different). If a good fit is only possible with a large dark facet, albedo variegation is likely. period_scan reports the dark facet area in percent for each trial period.
findings.source: DAMIT convexinv manual (convexinv_doc.pdf, v0.2.1)
findings.quote: There is a dark facet area that makes the whole set of facets convex. Always try to put it below 1% of the total area

findings.claim: DAMIT period_scan: DeltaP is about 0.5 P^2/Deltat; the scan step is p DeltaP with p < 1 (recommended 0.8); number of trial periods = 2 Deltat (P1 - P0)/(P0 P1)/p. It uses six initial poles per trial period. Uniqueness in the manual is only qualitative: one pole significantly better than all others, and 5-10 random initial poles for convexinv.
findings.source: DAMIT convexinv manual (convexinv_doc.pdf, v0.2.1)
findings.quote: The interval is scanned with the step p ∆P (always set p < 1, a recommended value is p = 0.8).
