A web-search snippet said its sparse data were weighted one third of the dense data, but I could not confirm this. What I can confirm comes from later papers by the same group: Hanus 2011 says the USNO data had about 8-10% uncertainty and gave 24 models. For "Durech 2010/2011" I used Durech 2016 (Lowell), Durech 2018 (Lowell + WISE) and Hanus 2016 instead. I also added Hanus 2021 (ASAS-SN), which is the closest match to your noise levels.

DAMIT v0.2.1 source code (my own reading of the code, not from any paper):
- period_scan.c uses six fixed starting poles: (0,0), (180,0), (90,60), (240,60), (90,-60), (240,-60). The papers use 10 isotropic poles.
- It steps uniformly in frequency: step = 0.5/(JDmax-JDmin)/24 x p, in 1/h.
- Every lightcurve's per-point sigma is set to that lightcurve's observed mean brightness. A Weight array is declared but never used. So the public code has no input for per-observatory weights (the 0.3 / 0.15 / 0.1 of Hanus 2011/2016, or w = 0.01 of Durech 2019). To use such weights the sigma assignment would have to be modified.
- For lightcurves flagged calibrated (1), the model is not rescaled per lightcurve. Zero-point or band offsets between observatories (V, G, o, c, TESS) are therefore not absorbed and will leave systematic residuals.
- For lightcurves flagged relative (0), each lightcurve gets its own free scale. A multi-apparition per-observatory sparse set flagged 0 keeps its internal brightness changes across apparitions and phase angles but gets a free offset. This is effectively what ATLAS did with its free c-o colour scale.

Inconsistencies in the papers:
- Durech 2019 says it adopted k = 3 for convex models, but only k = 1, 1/2 and 1/3 were tested; 1/3 is probably meant.
- Durech 2019 gives 762 new models in the abstract and 775 in Sect. 2.4. 775 minus the 13 rejected afterwards gives 762.
- DeltaP is defined differently: P^2/T in Hanus & Durech 2012, but 0.5 P^2/T in the DAMIT manual, Durech 2016 and Durech 2023. So "0.5 DeltaP" in Hanus & Durech 2012 equals "1.0 DeltaP" in the DAMIT convention.

Settings that recur across these papers, applied to the ~177-asteroid MPC set:
- Data grouping: one sparse lightcurve per observatory (and per band), at least about 30 points. Reject observatories whose phase-curve residual median is about 0.2 mag or more; Hanus 2011 dropped 691, 704, 608, 644, 683 and H07.
- Outliers: clip at 2.5 rms around a fitted linear-exponential phase function, optionally also cutting points with errors above 0.15 mag.
- Period scan: 2-100 h (2-1000 h or more for slow rotators, with Pmin > 50 h checked to 1000 h), step 0.5-0.8 DeltaP with DeltaP = 0.5 P^2/T, about 10 initial poles.
- Run three period searches: convex n = 3, convex n = 6, and ellipsoid.
- Uniqueness: chi2_tr = (1 + k sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min with k = 0.5 (Lowell + WISE, ASAS-SN) or 1 (Gaia). The older rules were a fixed 5% (Lowell 2016) or 10% (Hanus 2011).
- Poles: at most 2, with |dbeta| < 50 deg and dlambda 120-240 deg; otherwise report a partial model if the beta spread is 25 deg or less.
- Shape checks: inertia ratio below 1.1 (or spin axis within 30 deg of the maximum-inertia axis), dark facet below 1%, and a jackknife or bootstrap rerun that recovers the same period.
- Without a period prior, Durech 2016 accepted only P < 20 h.

What to expect:
- Success rates: about 1% or less for Lowell alone, about 1.2% for Lowell + WISE, about 3% for ATLAS, about 15% for ASAS-SN with errors below 0.15 mag.
- False positives that pass all tests: a few percent (0.6% for Gaia DR3).
- Pole agreement with dense-lightcurve models: mean 12-15 deg, median 9-13 deg (Lowell-based); about 20 deg mean for Gaia DR2.

On your ellipsoid-vs-convex question: these papers consistently find that the ellipsoid is the better period finder for noisy sparse data. Of the 662 new Lowell + WISE models, 513 came from the ellipsoid period search. Convex shapes are then used for the pole and shape. Sparse-only convex shapes come out angular with sharp edges, and slightly less elongated than DAMIT models. The improvement over an ellipsoid should mainly show for lightcurves that are not simple double sinusoids (Durech & Hanus 2023).

results.claim: Hanus et al. 2011 fitted each per-observatory sparse lightcurve from AstDyS with a phase curve and rejected any observatory whose median or 'FWHM' residual was about 0.2 mag or more. Their Table 1 residual medians: 689 0.15, 703 0.19, E12 0.15, G96 0.17, 950 0.15, 699 0.18, Hipparcos 0.11. Rejected: 691 0.24, 704 0.42, 608 0.27, 644 0.24, 683 0.20, H07 0.23.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134; arXiv:1104.4114 (ar5iv Sect. 2.1, Table 1); DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201116738 (checked on Crossref: correct title, A&A 530 A134)
results.evidence: Sect. 2.1: the analysis covered 13 observatories that had data for more than ~50 asteroids, taken from the first 10,000 numbered asteroids, using lightcurves with at least 30 points. Each sparse lightcurve was fitted with Eq. 1. The text says observatories with a high median or FWHM (about 0.2 mag or more 'for both') are unsuitable. All 13 medians match the claim exactly. However, the FWHM rule was not applied mechanically. Table 1 FWHM values: 689 0.12, 703 0.16, E12 0.16, G96 0.22, 950 0.11, 699 0.11, Hip 0.10; zero-weight 608 0.20, 644 0.22, 683 0.25, 691 0.22, 704 0.17, H07 0.18. G96 has FWHM 0.22 but was kept with weight 0.1, and 704 has FWHM 0.17 but was rejected because its median is 0.42. In practice the split follows the median: every kept observatory has a median of 0.19 or less and every rejected one 0.20 or more. The paper says the weights were estimated from both the medians and the FWHMs. Side note: the arXiv abstract page lists an unrelated 'related DOI' (an Icarus radar paper); the A&A DOI in the claim is the correct one.
results.corrected_claim: Hanus et al. 2011 fitted each sparse lightcurve (13 observatories with data for more than ~50 asteroids, first 10,000 numbered asteroids) with Eq. 1 and judged each observatory by the median and FWHM of its rms residuals. The paper says observatories with a high median or FWHM (about 0.2 mag or more) are unsuitable, but in Table 1 the accept/reject split follows the median (kept 0.19 or less, rejected 0.20 or more). G96 was kept (weight 0.1) despite FWHM 0.22. The medians are as listed in the claim.

results.claim: Hanus et al. 2011 weighted each observatory relative to dense lightcurves, which had weight 1 and an assumed accuracy of about 0.02 mag. Weights: 689 USNO 0.3, Hipparcos 0.3, 703 CSS 0.15, 950 La Palma 0.15, 699 LONEOS 0.1, E12 Siding Spring 0.1, G96 Mt Lemmon 0.1. All other observatories, including 691, 704, 608 and 644, got weight 0.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2011, arXiv:1104.4114, Sect. 2.1 and Table 1
results.evidence: Table 1 weights: 689 0.3, Hip 0.3, 703 0.15, 950 0.15, 699 0.1, E12 0.1, G96 0.1. Weight 0: 608, 644, 683, 691, 704, H07. The text says only the seven observatories with non-zero weights were accurate enough to use. Weights are relative to dense data, which has unity weight, and the typical accuracy of dense lightcurves is assumed to be about 0.02 mag.

results.claim: Sparse data are kept as one 'sparse lightcurve' per observatory per asteroid. Hanus 2011 required at least 30 points, computed the geometry, corrected for light-time and reduced brightness to 1 AU (i.e. calibrated data). A typical asteroid had 2-4 such lightcurves covering about 10-15 years.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2011, arXiv:1104.4114, Sects. 2 and 2.1
results.evidence: Sect. 2.1: data were extracted for the first 10,000 numbered asteroids when a single lightcurve had at least 30 points. The processing computed the geometry (astrocentric ecliptic coordinates of the Sun and Earth), corrected for light-time, normalized brightness to 1 AU from both the Sun and the Earth, and excluded clear outliers. End of Sect. 2: a given asteroid typically has 2-4 sparse lightcurves from different observatories, covering the last ~10-15 years. Note: Hanus 2011 does not use the word 'calibrated' here; that label is the claimant's inference. It matches the DAMIT manual, where 'calibrated' means brightness reduced to unit distances.

results.claim: To estimate each observatory's quality, Hanus 2011 fitted every sparse lightcurve with f(alpha) = cos^2(alpha/2) [a exp(-alpha/b) + c alpha + d], with a, b, c, d free, and built histograms of the rms residuals per observatory.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2011, arXiv:1104.4114, Sect. 2.1, Eq. 1, Fig. 1
results.evidence: Eq. 1 is exactly f(alpha) = cos^2(alpha/2)[a exp(-alpha/b) + c alpha + d], with a, b, c, d as free parameters. A histogram of rms residuals against this model was built for each observatory (Fig. 1 shows 689, 691, 703 and E12). The mode, FWHM and median are given in Table 1.

results.claim: Most survey photometry in AstDyS/MPC is quantized to 0.1 mag. Hanus 2011 notes the mean lightcurve amplitude is about 0.3 mag and 19% of asteroids have amplitude of 0.5 mag or more, so 0.1-mag data can still constrain spin and shape for many objects. The USNO (689) data used by Durech et al. 2009 had about 8-10% uncertainty.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2011, arXiv:1104.4114, Sect. 2
results.evidence: Sect. 2: in most cases magnitudes are given to one decimal place, so accuracy is 0.1 mag at best. Using LCDB amplitudes for ~2500 asteroids, the mean amplitude is ~0.3 mag and 19% have 0.5 mag or more. The paper concludes that ~0.1 mag photometry carries enough information for a significant number of asteroids. The USNO-Flagstaff data used by Durech et al. 2009 had a typical uncertainty of ~8-10%.

results.claim: Hanus 2011 (and Hanus & Durech 2012) defined a unique solution as follows. (i) The best period has at least 10% lower chi2 than all other periods. (ii) Only one pole has at least 10% lower chi2 than the others, apart from the lambda+-180 deg mirror. (iii) The solution passes the additional tests.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2011, arXiv:1104.4114, Sect. 3.1; Hanus & Durech 2012, arXiv:1301.7205, footnote 5
results.evidence: Hanus 2011 Sect. 3.1 gives the three-part definition: (i) at least 10% lower chi2 than all other periods in the scanned interval; (ii) only one pole at least 10% lower, with a possible lambda+-180 ambiguity; (iii) passes the additional tests of Sect. 3.3. Hanus & Durech 2012, footnote 5, repeats the same definition word for word ('all our additional tests').

results.claim: Hanus 2011 scan windows: centred on the LCDB period with half-width +-1%, +-5% or +-20% of P for reliability codes 4, 3 and 2; half and double periods were tested afterwards. Without a prior period they scanned 2-30 h.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2011, arXiv:1104.4114, Sects. 1 and 3.1
results.evidence: Sect. 3.1: the interval is centred on the reported LCDB period with a range of +-1%, +-5% and +-20% of P for reliability codes 4, 3 and 2. Half and double periods were tested later. Sect. 1: with only sparse data and no dense lightcurves, the whole expected interval of 2-30 hours must be scanned.

results.claim: Hanus 2011 additional tests: (1) reject a model if the spin axis is more than 30 deg from the maximum-inertia axis, with an exception for some elongated shapes; (2) reject if a fit at 2P or P/2 has chi2 below 1.1 chi2(P); (3) for sparse-only models, rerun with 90% of the points; (4) compare with existing DAMIT models; (5) invert 10 'mock' objects.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2011, arXiv:1104.4114, Sect. 3.3
results.evidence: Sect. 3.3 lists five tests. The first two were run for all models; the other three only for models derived from sparse data alone. (1) Reject if the angle between the spin axis and the maximum-inertia axis exceeds +-30 deg. Exception: elongated models whose sizes along the rotation axis and along the minimal perpendicular axis are similar. (2) The half/double test was run only when the period was in doubt (low LCDB reliability code): search near 2P and P/2 and reject the model if chi2 there is below 1.1 chi2(P). (3) Randomly reduce the sparse points to 90% and invert again. (4) Compare with existing DAMIT models. (5) Ten mock objects per sparse-only model. The claim omits that test 2 was conditional.
results.corrected_claim: Hanus 2011 tests: (1) inertia check, rejecting models where the spin axis is more than 30 deg from the maximum-inertia axis (with an exception for some elongated shapes); (2) only when the LCDB period was in doubt, reject if the chi2 near 2P or P/2 is below 1.1 chi2(P). Tests 1-2 were applied to all models. Tests 3-5 were applied only to sparse-only models: (3) rerun with 90% of the sparse points, (4) comparison with DAMIT models, (5) inversion of 10 mock objects.

results.claim: Hanus 2011 inverted about 2300 data sets (about 900 sparse-only) and obtained 80 new unique models (16 from sparse data alone) plus 30 partial models (mean beta reported when the beta dispersion was below 50 deg). All 16 sparse-only models of asteroids already in DAMIT were similar to the DAMIT models. Mock tests gave pole uncertainty of about +-10 deg and period uncertainty of about 0.1 of the spacing between local minima.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2011, arXiv:1104.4114, Sects. 3.1 and 3.3
results.evidence: Sect. 3.1: data sets for ~2300 asteroids, ~900 of them sparse-only. 80 new unique models, 16 based only on sparse data. 30 partial models, where beta is the mean of all solutions if the dispersion is below 50 deg, with Delta = |beta_max - beta_min|/2. Sect. 3.3: 16 asteroids already in DAMIT were modelled from sparse data, and similar models were obtained for all 16. Mock objects gave a typical pole uncertainty of +-10 deg and a period uncertainty of ~0.1 times the difference between two local minima. Note: Sect. 3.1 separately quotes a pole uncertainty of +-10-20 deg for the new models.

results.claim: Catalina (703) sparse data alone, typical accuracy about 12%: of 185 asteroids with at least 50 CSS points and an existing model, 13 gave a 'unique' solution, but only 7 of those agreed with the independent model. Six were formally unique but had the wrong period.
results.source: Hanus & Durech 2012, Planet. Space Sci. 73 (2012) 75-79 (arXiv journal-ref); arXiv:1301.7205, Sects. 2-3 (Test 1)
results.evidence: Sect. 2: the typical photometric accuracy of CSS data was ~12%. Test 1: at least 50 CSS points were available for 185 asteroids that already had models. 13 gave unique solutions; only 7 agreed with the model from other data. The other six were formally correct but had periods different from the expected ones.

results.claim: Hanus & Durech 2012 used period step Pstep = 0.8 DeltaP with DeltaP = P^2/T. After testing shape resolutions n = 2-6 and steps 0.8 and 0.5 DeltaP, they recommend n = 6 with Pstep = 0.5 DeltaP and, if a unique solution appears, a rerun with n = 3 and 0.5 DeltaP. Wrong 'unique' solutions never appeared for n = 2 or 3.
results.source: Hanus & Durech 2012, arXiv:1301.7205, Test 3 (Eq. 1, Table 1) and Discussion
results.evidence: Eq. 1 defines DeltaP = P^2/T, and the standard step was Pstep = 0.8 DeltaP. Table 1 tests n = 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 at both 0.8 and 0.5 DeltaP. Discussion: use n = 6 and Pstep = 0.5 DeltaP; if a unique solution appears, rerun with n = 3 and 0.5 DeltaP. Incorrect models gave unique solutions only rarely at other settings and never for n = 2 or 3, which Table 1 confirms. Caution: this DeltaP (P^2/T) is twice the DAMIT-manual DeltaP (0.5 P^2/dt). So 0.5 DeltaP here equals 1.0 DAMIT DeltaP, and 0.8 DeltaP here equals 1.6 DAMIT DeltaP.

results.claim: For correct CSS-only solutions, the period dispersion across resolutions was below DeltaP (about 1e-3 h for P = 10 h over a 10-year span). Pole latitude scattered by about 20 deg or less, while pole longitude often scattered by 50 deg or more.
results.source: Hanus & Durech 2012, arXiv:1301.7205, Conclusions
results.evidence: Conclusions: correct period solutions were stable across resolutions n. The period dispersion was typically below DeltaP, which is ~1e-3 h for P = 10 h and a 10-year span. The pole-latitude dispersion was usually about 20 deg or less; the longitude dispersion was often about 50 deg or more. This is partly due to high-latitude poles and low shape resolution. The paper says 'typically' lower than DeltaP.

results.claim: Hanus et al. 2013 used sparse data from 689, 703 and 950 with a priori LCDB periods, or 2-100 h when the period was unknown. Sparse-only solutions had to be stable at both n = 3 and n = 6, the typical n being 6, i.e. 49 shape parameters. Results: 119 combined models and 20 CSS-only models. Quoted pole uncertainty is 10-20 deg for combined models and 20-40 deg for CSS-only models.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2013, A&A 551, A67; arXiv:1301.6943 (abstract, Sects. 2, 2.1 footnote 9, Conclusions, Table 2 note); DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201220701 (listed on arXiv)
results.evidence: Abstract and Sect. 2: sparse data came from 689, 703 and 950. LCDB periods were used as a priori information; if the period was unknown or insecure, 2-100 h was searched. Footnote 9: there are (n+1)^2 shape parameters with typical n = 6, and the correct solution had to be stable at both n = 3 and n = 6. The figure of 49 is arithmetic, not stated. Results: 119 combined models and 20 CSS-only models. Pole uncertainty: 10-20 deg for combined models (Conclusions) and 20-40 deg in the Table 2 note for CSS-only models.

results.claim: Hanus et al. 2016 weights relative to dense data (weight 1): USNO 689 = 0.3, CSS 703 = 0.15, and 0.1 for the whole Lowell re-calibrated set. They note that one weight for a mix of observatories over- or under-weights individual asteroids. 57 of their 250 models were from USNO+CSS sparse data alone, with 2-1000 h typically scanned.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2016, A&A 586, A108; arXiv:1510.07422, Sects. 2 and 4.2
results.evidence: Sect. 2: AstDyS sparse data from 689 and 703 were weighted 0.3 and 0.15 relative to dense data (unity weight). Lowell data were weighted 0.1. Sect. 4.2: because Lowell data mix several observatories, a single weight can overestimate some asteroids and underestimate others. 57 of the 250 models are based only on USNO and CSS sparse data, with a period interval of 2-1000 h typically scanned.

results.claim: Hanus 2016 typical pole uncertainties: 5 deg or less for large multi-apparition dense data sets; 5-10 deg for dense plus sparse; 10-30 deg in beta (10-30 deg / cos beta in lambda) for few-apparition dense plus sparse, or sparse alone. Sparse-based shapes have many flat facets and sharp edges.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2016, arXiv:1510.07422, Sect. 3
results.evidence: Sect. 3 gives three tiers: (i) 5 deg or less in beta (5 deg/cos beta in lambda) for large multi-apparition dense data sets; (ii) ~5-10 deg for multi-apparition dense data combined with sparse data; (iii) ~10-30 deg in beta and ~10-30 deg/cos beta in lambda for few-apparition dense plus sparse data, or sparse data only. It also says shapes based mostly on sparse data usually have many flat facets with rather sharp edges.

results.claim: Durech et al. 2016 (Lowell database, 0.10-0.20 mag accuracy, about 480 points per asteroid for numbers below 10,000) scanned 2-100 h with 10 isotropic initial poles per trial period. That is 200,000-300,000 trial periods per asteroid (about a month on one CPU), run on Asteroids@home. With an LCDB prior: P +-5% for U = 3/3-, +-10% for U = 2+.
results.evidence: Sect. 2.1: accuracy is around 0.10-0.20 mag, with an average of ~480 points for asteroids numbered below 10,000 (~45 above 300,000). Sect. 2.2: the scan covers 2-100 h with ten isotropically distributed initial poles per trial period. A typical data set needs 200,000-300,000 trial periods, about a month on one CPU, so the work ran on Asteroids@home (Sect. 2.3). Sect. 2.5: P+-0.05P for U = 3 and 3-, P+-0.1P for U = 2+, applied to both convex and ellipsoid searches.

results.claim: Durech 2016 Test 1: the global minimum must be at least 5% lower than every chi2 outside Pmin +- 0.5 Pmin^2/DeltaT. The 5% level was tuned against DAMIT to give about 1% false positives. Test 2: the periods from n = 3 and n = 6 must agree. Test 3: without an LCDB prior, only Pmin < 20 h is accepted.
results.source: Durech et al. 2016, arXiv:1601.02909, Sect. 2.6 (tests 1-3)
results.evidence: Test 1: chi2 at Pmin must be at least 5% lower than all chi2 outside Pmin+-0.5Pmin^2/DeltaT. The 5% was chosen to maximise unique models while keeping false positives very low (~1%), judged against DAMIT. Test 2: for convex period scans, resolutions 3 and 6 must give Pmin agreeing within errors, and both must pass test 1. Test 3: only Pmin shorter than 20 h was accepted when there was no LCDB period.

results.claim: Durech 2016 pole and shape tests: at most two distinct poles (more than 30 deg apart) at least 5% deeper than the others; for a pair, |beta1 - beta2| < 50 deg and mod(|lambda1 - lambda2|, 180 deg) > 120 deg; moment of inertia about the principal axis over that about the rotation axis < 1.1; a bootstrap rerun must recover the same Pmin; then visual inspection.
results.source: Durech et al. 2016, arXiv:1601.02909, Sect. 2.6 (tests 4-8)
results.evidence: Test 4: no more than two distinct poles (more than 30 deg apart) with chi2 at least 5% deeper than other poles. Test 5: |beta1 - beta2| < 50 deg and mod(|lambda1 - lambda2|, 180 deg) > 120 deg, as written in the paper. Test 6: the inertia ratio (principal axis over actual rotation axis) must be below 1.1. Test 7: a bootstrapped data set, processed the same way, must give the same Pmin. Test 8: visual check of shapes, periodograms and fits.

results.claim: Durech 2016 results: Lowell data for the first 100,000 numbered asteroids gave about 600 models passing all tests, 328 of them new. Of 279 that overlap DAMIT, 275 had the same period and pole differences below 50 deg (mean 15 deg, median 13 deg). False positives were about a few percent, and models are biased toward elongated, high-amplitude bodies.
results.source: Durech et al. 2016, arXiv:1601.02909, abstract and Sects. 3.1-3.3
results.evidence: Sect. 3.1: ~600 models passed the tests and 279 were in DAMIT. Of these, 275 had the same period and pole differences below 50 deg, with a mean of 15 deg and a median of 13 deg. The false-positive frequency is 'around a few percent' and may be higher because of DAMIT's bias. Abstract: 328 new models from the first 100,000 numbered asteroids, heavily biased towards elongated, high-amplitude bodies. Sect. 3.3: almost all new models have amplitudes of about 0.3 mag or more.

results.claim: Durech 2016 also searched periods with a triaxial ellipsoid under geometric scattering, which is analytic and always rotates about its maximum-inertia axis, and then used that period to start convex inversion. Where convex models gave many equally good periods, the ellipsoid often gave a unique and correct one.
results.source: Durech et al. 2016, arXiv:1601.02909, Sect. 2.4
results.evidence: Sect. 2.4: a triaxial ellipsoid with geometric scattering (Kaasalainen & Durech 2007), whose brightness is computed analytically and so is much faster. All such shapes automatically rotate about the axis of largest inertia. The ellipsoid period is used as the starting point for convex inversion. In many cases where convex models give many equally good periods, the ellipsoid gives a unique and correct one. The paper says 'in many cases'.

results.claim: Durech et al. 2018 (Lowell + WISE) replaced the fixed 5% with a per-asteroid threshold chi2_tr = (1 + 0.5 sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min. nu = Ndata - Nparams, with Nparams = 3 spin + 3 phase-function + (n+1)^2 shape parameters (or 2 for an ellipsoid). The old 5% level corresponds to nu = 200.
results.source: Durech, Hanus & Ali-Lagoa 2018, A&A 617, A57; arXiv:1807.02083, Sect. 2.4
results.evidence: Sect. 2.4: the fixed threshold chi2_tr = 1.05 chi2_min was replaced by chi2_tr = (1 + 0.5 sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min. nu is the number of data points minus the number of parameters: 3 spin, 3 phase-function, and (n+1)^2 convex shape parameters or 2 ellipsoid parameters. The factor 1/2 is an empirical adjustment. The old 5% corresponds to nu = 200, and indeed 0.5*sqrt(2/200) = 0.05.

results.claim: Durech 2018 pipeline: scan 2-100 h independently with convex n = 3, convex n = 6 and ellipsoids. The unique periods from n = 3 and n = 6 must agree. If Pmin > 50 h, also scan 100-1000 h. More than two poles under chi2_tr gives a partial model, reported if the beta values span 50 deg or less (Delta <= 25 deg). Two poles must differ by less than 50 deg in beta and 120-240 deg in lambda. Then an inertia check and a visual check.
results.source: Durech et al. 2018, arXiv:1807.02083, Sect. 2.4 (steps 1-8, Fig. 3) and Sect. 3.3
results.evidence: Steps: (1) scan 2-100 h independently with convex n = 3, convex n = 6 and ellipsoids; (2) uniqueness against chi2_tr; (3) the n = 3 and n = 6 unique periods must agree within errors; (4) if the period exceeds 50 h, rescan 100-1000 h; (5) more than two poles under chi2_tr gives a partial model; (6) two poles must have dbeta < 50 deg and dlambda 120-240 deg; (7) check rotation about the shortest axis; (8) visual check. Sect. 3.3: partial models are listed only when beta is confined within 50 deg, so Delta is 25 deg or less.

results.claim: Durech 2018: ellipsoid period search is about 100 times faster and more efficient than convex search, because flexible convex models can fit a wrong period with a non-physical shape. Of the 662 new models, 169 came from convex period search, 513 from ellipsoids and 20 from both. After the period is found, the pole search is done with convex shapes.
results.source: Durech et al. 2018, arXiv:1807.02083, Sects. 2.3 and 3.2
results.evidence: Sect. 2.3: the ellipsoid has two shape parameters (a/c, b/c) and analytic brightness, making it about one hundred times faster than convex polyhedra. It is more efficient at finding the correct period because flexible convex models can formally fit an incorrect period with a nonphysical shape, and the inertia check runs only after the fact. After the ellipsoid period is found, the pole search switches back to convex shapes. Sect. 3.2: 662 new models (169 convex, 513 ellipsoids, 20 overlapping; 169 + 513 - 20 = 662).

results.claim: Durech 2018 results: about 75,000 asteroids gave 908 unique models (about 1.2%) plus 789 partial models. Of 246 already in DAMIT, 237 had the correct period, with mean pole difference 12 deg and median 9 deg. The convex models were slightly less elongated than DAMIT ones (mean a/b and b/c ratios DAMIT/ours about 1.06).
results.source: Durech et al. 2018, arXiv:1807.02083, abstract and Sects. 3, 3.1, 3.3
results.evidence: Sect. 3: ~75,000 asteroids gave 908 unique models, 246 of them already known. Sect. 3.1: of the 246, five had slightly different periods (neighbouring local minima, relative difference ~1e-4), four had completely different periods, and 237 were correct. Pole difference: mean 12 deg, median 9 deg. Mean (a/b)_DAMIT/(a/b)_ours ~1.06 (sd 0.13) and (b/c) ratio 1.06 (sd 0.18), so the new models are slightly less elongated. Sect. 3.3: 789 partial models. The figure of 1.2% is derived (908/75,000) and not stated in the paper.

results.claim: Gaia DR2 inversion used chi2_tr = (1 + sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min, i.e. factor 1 instead of 1/2. Parameters: p = 6 for the ellipsoid (P, lambda, beta, a linear phase slope, a/c, b/c) and p = 20 for a convex n = 3 model. Only the linear phase term was fitted because Gaia phase angles are above 10 deg. Periodograms were rejected unless every RMS exceeded 0.005 mag and only one period had RMS below 0.01.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91; arXiv:1810.04485, Sect. 2.2
results.evidence: Sect. 2.2: chi2_tr = (1 + sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min, with no factor 1/2 compared with Durech 2018. Ellipsoid p = 6: P, lambda, beta, a linear phase slope, a/c, b/c. Only the linear phase part was fitted because the phase angle is almost always above 10 deg. Convex order and degree 3 means 16 shape parameters, so p = 20 in total. Spin/shape models were made only for N > 20. Periodograms were kept only if all RMS values exceeded 0.005 mag and only one period had RMS below 0.01.

results.claim: Durech & Hanus 2018 gave all Gaia DR2 points equal weight and ignored the individual errors, since model errors exceed the 1-2% photometric errors. They report that ground-based sparse surveys give robust models for less than 1% of asteroids.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, arXiv:1810.04485, Sect. 2
results.evidence: Sect. 2: all points had the same weight and individual errors were ignored. Relative formal errors are below 2% for 90% of points, and model errors (simplified shape and scattering, uniform albedo) are larger. The Gaia Collaboration estimated DR2 asteroid photometry accuracy as probably better than 1-2%. The paper cites Durech et al. 2016 for a success rate below one percent from ground-based surveys.

results.claim: Gaia DR2 (10-50 points per asteroid): correct-period fraction exceeds 0.5 only when N > 30. 173 models were derived, 44 of them already in DAMIT, with mean pole difference 20 deg and 7 outliers above 60 deg (mostly neighbouring local minima in period). n = 3 convex shapes are unrealistic, with sharp edges.
results.evidence: DR2 has from a few up to 50 points per object, and 5413 asteroids with N of 10 or more were processed. Sect. 2.1: the fraction of correct periods (within +-5% of LCDB periods with U of 3 or more) rises above 0.5 when N > 30. Sect. 2.3: 173 models, 44 in DAMIT, mean pole difference 20 deg. Seven outliers above 60 deg: five neighbouring local minima, one completely different period, and one (2802 Weisell) where the DAMIT model was wrong. Sect. 2.2: n = 3 shapes are often unrealistic, with sharp edges and triangular pole-on silhouettes. Spin/shape models were derived only for N > 20.

results.claim: Durech et al. 2019 joint Gaia DR2 + Lowell fit: chi2_rel = sum over Gaia residuals^2 + w * sum over Lowell residuals^2, with w = 0.01 (0.1-mag versus 0.01-mag errors); w = 0.05 and 0.1 were also tested. Threshold chi2_tr = (1 + k sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min with k = 1, 1/2, 1/3. For w = 0.01, convex models gave 287, 522, 641 unique periods with 87%, 86%, 83% correct against LCDB (within 10%); ellipsoids gave 710, 997, 1215 with 90%, 85%, 78%.
results.source: Durech, Hanus & Vanco 2019, A&A 631, A2 (DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201936341 via Crossref); arXiv:1909.09395, Sect. 2.1, Eq. 1, Table 1
results.evidence: Eq. 1: chi2_rel = sum_Gaia (Lobs - Lmodel)^2 + w sum_Lowell (Lobs - Lmodel)^2. w = 0.01 follows from 0.1 mag (Lowell) versus 0.01 mag (Gaia); w = 0.05 and 0.1 were also tested. Threshold (1 + k sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min with k = 1, 1/2, 1/3. Table 1 at w = 0.01: convex 287/87%, 522/86%, 641/83%; ellipsoids 710/90%, 997/85%, 1215/78%. 'Correct' means within +-10% of LCDB periods with U of 3 or more.

results.claim: Durech 2019 states the adopted values as w = 0.01, 'k = 3' for convex models and k = 1 for ellipsoids. Since only k = 1, 1/2 and 1/3 were tested, 'k = 3' is probably a typo for 1/3. About 15% of the accepted periods were wrong, but most of these failed later checks. 1142 models passed all checks; of 367 in DAMIT, 4 had completely different periods and 11 sat in a neighbouring local minimum with poles more than 60 deg off.
results.source: Durech et al. 2019, arXiv:1909.09395, Sects. 2.1 and 2.3
results.evidence: Sect. 2.1 of the arXiv text does literally say w = 0.01, k = 3 for convex models and k = 1 for ellipsoids, while Table 1 tests only k = 1, 1/2, 1/3. The 'typo for 1/3' reading is the claimant's inference: plausible, but the paper does not state it, and the A&A full text could not be checked (HTTP 403). About 15% of periods were incorrect, but most failed later checks (convex vs ellipsoid periodograms, visual fits, shortest-axis rotation). Sect. 2.3: 1142 models passed all tests and 367 were in DAMIT. Four had completely different periods. Eleven had very similar periods (~1e-4) in different local minima, with poles more than 60 deg apart; the paper says it was unclear which model was correct, since many DAMIT models there were sparse-only.

results.claim: For ATLAS, Durech et al. 2020 fitted a linear-exponential phase function, as in Hanus 2011, and clipped points deviating by more than 2.5 rms, which removed about 15% of points. They kept asteroids with at least 100 observations (about 98,000).
results.source: Durech et al. 2020, A&A 643, A59; arXiv:2010.01820, Sect. 2
results.evidence: Sect. 2: following Hanus 2011, a linear-exponential phase function was fitted and points beyond a limit were removed. The limit was set at 2.5 rms after tests, removing about 15% of points on average. Afterwards only asteroids with at least 100 observations were kept, about 98,000.

results.claim: ATLAS 2015-2018 data: periods 2-1000 h were scanned with both convex and ellipsoid models. Only about 5000 of about 100,000 asteroids gave a reliable sidereal period on the full interval. With an LCDB prior the window was +-5% (U = 3/3-), +-10% (U = 2+) or +-20% (U = 2).
results.source: Durech et al. 2020, arXiv:2010.01820, Sects. 2-3
results.evidence: Data run from June 2015 to October 2018. Sect. 3: both full convex inversion (Asteroids@home) and the ellipsoid model were used, and periodograms covered the whole 2-1000 h interval for all asteroids. A reliable sidereal period was found for only about five thousand of almost a hundred thousand. LCDB (November 2018 version) windows: +-5% for U = 3 or 3-, +-10% for U = 2+, +-20% for U = 2.

results.claim: Scattering law used in the ATLAS work: S = f(alpha) mu mu0 [1/(mu + mu0) + c] with c = 0.1 fixed, and f(alpha) = A0 exp(-alpha/D) + k alpha + 1 with A0, D, k optimized and k constrained non-positive. The two filters (c, o) share one phase function, and the c-o colour is fitted as a free scale factor between the per-filter data sets.
results.source: Durech et al. 2020, arXiv:2010.01820, Sect. 4.3 (Eqs. 1-2)
results.evidence: Eq. 1: S = f(alpha) mu mu0 (1/(mu+mu0) + c), with c = 0.1 constant. Eq. 2: f = A0 exp(-alpha/D) + k alpha + 1, with A0, D and k optimized. The slope cannot be positive, and this is constrained during optimization. The phase function was assumed the same for both filters. A test with separate k_c and k_o gave a mean k_c - k_o of -0.023. The c-o colour is a free scale factor between the two filter data sets (the (673) Edda example).

results.claim: ATLAS results: about 2750 unique models (950 already known; 1800 new, of which 705 full, 191 full with an LCDB prior, 671 partial, 225 partial with a prior), i.e. under 3% of about 100,000. Errors came from 100 bootstrap resamplings. Mean rms residual was 0.08 mag for P < 20 h and 0.12 mag for P > 100 h.
results.source: Durech et al. 2020, arXiv:2010.01820, abstract, Sects. 4, 4.1, 4.5, Conclusions
results.evidence: Sect. 4: about 2750 unique models, about 950 previously known, and 1800 new: 705 full, 191 with a prior period, 671 partial, 225 partial with a prior. Conclusions: fewer than 3000 models from about 100,000 asteroids. Sect. 4.1: one hundred bootstrap samples per model, with uncertainties taken as standard deviations. Sect. 4.5: mean rms is 0.08 mag for P < 20 h and 0.12 mag for P > 100 h (similar for medians).

results.claim: Gaia DR3: 2-10,000 h scanned with step 0.8 DeltaP for convex models and 0.5 DeltaP for ellipsoids, where DeltaP = 0.5 P^2/T (uniform in frequency, step 0.4/T). Convex shape n = 3 (288 facets, 15 free coefficients). Minimum relative error 0.01. Only the phase slope k was fitted; a0 = 0.5, d = 0.1 and c = 0.1 were fixed. Sample: asteroids with at least 21 points.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24; arXiv:2305.10798, Sect. 2
results.evidence: Sect. 2 confirms each setting. Periodograms cover 2-10,000 h with a step of 0.8 DeltaP, where DeltaP = 0.5 P^2/T, equivalent to a uniform frequency step of 0.4/T. Ellipsoids used a step of 0.5 DeltaP. Convex shapes are spherical harmonics of order and degree 3 on 288 surface elements; a0 is fixed, leaving 15 optimized coefficients. Minimum relative error 0.01. Only k was optimized; a0 = 0.5, d = 0.1 and c = 0.1 were fixed. The sample was the 60,945 asteroids with 21 or more observations.

results.claim: Gaia DR3 period uniqueness: every other period must have chi2 > (1 + sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min, and every local minimum must have RMS > 0.01. Convex funnel: 14,192 unique periods, then 11,854 with 1-2 poles, 8820 with inertia ratio < 1.1, and 8230 with |dbeta| <= 50 deg and dlambda >= 120 deg. Ellipsoid funnel: 16,010, then 9910, 7873, 7122.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, arXiv:2305.10798, Sect. 2
results.evidence: Sect. 2: unique period means all other periods have chi2 > (1 + sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min and the RMS of all local minima exceeds 0.01. Convex funnel: 14,192, then 11,854 (one or two poles), then 8820 (successful Minkowski conversion and inertia ratio below 1.1), then 8230. At the last step, two-pole solutions with latitude differences above 50 deg and longitude differences below 120 deg were rejected. Ellipsoid funnel: 16,010, then 9910, 7873, 7122.

results.claim: Gaia DR3 stability test: 10 jackknife runs, each removing 10% of the points, and at least 9 of 10 must return the original period within 0.1%. Final 8596 models. The false-solution rate against LCDB U = 3 periods was about 0.6% (5 of 848). Success rate rises from a few percent at N = 21 to about 40% at N around 60.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, arXiv:2305.10798, Sects. 2.1, 2.2 and results
results.evidence: Sect. 2.1: data split into ten parts, one tenth removed per run, ten runs. Kept if all ten periods matched within 0.1%, or at most one disagreed. This gave 6269 convex and 5784 ellipsoid models, combined to 8602 after removing 20 conflicts. Sect. 2.2: 848 LCDB periods with U = 3; five DR3 periods were wrong, about 0.6%. Later, 6 objects were excluded after the LCDB and DAMIT comparisons, giving 8596 final models. Success rate: a few percent at N = 21, rising to about 40% around N = 60.

results.claim: Durech & Hanus 2023 list the ellipsoid's advantages: fewer parameters, physically correct rotation, no false half-period solutions, about 100 times faster. Its limit is lightcurves that are not simple double sinusoids. Of 1324 DR3 models also in DAMIT, 33 periods disagreed, and in most of those the DAMIT model, often built from Lowell sparse data alone, was the wrong one.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, arXiv:2305.10798, Sects. 2 and 2.4
results.evidence: Sect. 2 lists the ellipsoid's advantages: two shape parameters, rotation always about the shortest axis, no false half-period solutions, and analytic brightness that is about a hundred times faster. It is insufficient when the lightcurve departs significantly from a double sinusoid. Sect. 2.4: 1324 asteroids also in DAMIT, of which 33 had different periods. In most cases the DAMIT solutions are likely wrong; they are usually sparse-only and often Lowell-based. Only two of the 33 DR3 solutions were clearly wrong, and these were excluded.

results.claim: ASAS-SN V-band, Hanus et al. 2021: 2-1500 h scanned in steps of 0.5 DeltaP, with DeltaP/P = 0.5 P/T, and 10 isotropic initial poles. At least 60 points were required, since the model has 55 parameters (49 shape at n = 6, 3 spin, 3 phase). Threshold chi2_tr = (1 + p sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min, with p = 0.5 for convex and p = 0.6 for ellipsoids chosen against LCDB (about 3% inconsistent).
results.evidence: Sect. 3.1: convex inversion was applied to asteroids with MORE THAN 60 measurements (5283 asteroids), reflecting 55 free parameters (49 shape, 3 rotation, 3 phase). The scan covers 2-1500 h in steps of 0.5 DeltaP, with DeltaP/P = (1/2)(P/T), and ten isotropic initial poles per trial period. Eq. 3 is chi2_tr = (1 + p sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min. Sect. 3.2: p = 0.5 for convex and p = 0.6 for ellipsoids were chosen against LCDB periods flagged 3 or 3-. About 3% of convex periods disagree with LCDB; the ellipsoid rate is about 2% higher.
results.corrected_claim: Hanus et al. 2021 (ASAS-SN): 2-1500 h scanned in steps of 0.5 DeltaP, with DeltaP/P = 0.5 P/T, and 10 isotropic initial poles. Asteroids needed more than 60 points, because the model has 55 parameters (49 shape at n = 6, 3 spin, 3 phase). Threshold chi2_tr = (1 + p sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min, with p = 0.5 for convex and p = 0.6 for ellipsoids, chosen against LCDB flag 3/3- periods. About 3% of convex periods disagree with LCDB; the ellipsoid rate is about 2% higher.

results.claim: ASAS-SN preprocessing: drop points more than 0.7 mag from the predicted magnitude; fit the phase function and clip at 2.5 sigma (linear part only if 30 or fewer points or no low-phase data); keep only points with errors below 0.15 mag (about 30% removed). Result: 760 unique models from 5283 asteroids (about 15%, versus about 3% for ATLAS/Gaia DR2 and 1% or less for Lowell). Poles rarely differ from DAMIT by more than 30 deg.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2021, arXiv:2107.10027, Sects. 2 and 3.3
results.evidence: Sect. 2: points more than 0.7 mag from the Miriade-predicted V magnitude are removed. Eq. 1 is fitted and 2.5 sigma clipping applied. With roughly 30 or fewer points, or poor low-phase sampling (alpha < 10 deg), only the linear part is used. Only points with accuracy better than 0.15 mag are kept. Together these steps removed 30% of points on average. Sect. 3.3: 760 unique solutions from 5283 asteroids, about 15%, versus ~3% for ATLAS and Gaia DR2 and 1% or less for Lowell (alone or with WISE). Pole differences from DAMIT are rarely larger than 30 deg.

results.claim: The Asteroids IV review states the basic principle: an internally calibrated sparse data set is treated as one very long, sparsely sampled lightcurve. Current surveys reach accuracy scarcely better than 0.1 mag, and for noisy or limited sparse data a triaxial ellipsoid is usually enough to find the period and spin.
results.source: Durech et al. 2015, Asteroids IV; arXiv:1502.04816 (sparse-data paragraph of the lightcurve-inversion section); DOI 10.2458/azu_uapress_9780816532131-ch010 (Crossref title 'Asteroid Models from Multiple Data Sources'; page number not verified)
results.evidence: The review says an internally calibrated sparse data set can be used like a standard lightcurve that is extremely long and very sparsely sampled (citing Kaasalainen 2004). Current surveys give accuracy scarcely better than 0.1 mag, against a typical amplitude of 0.3 mag. With noisy sparse data or few points, a triaxial ellipsoid is usually enough to derive the correct period and spin (citing Cellino et al.).

results.claim: DAMIT convexinv input format: each lightcurve block starts with the number of points and a flag, 0 = relative or 1 = calibrated. Calibrated brightness is in intensity units reduced to unit distances. Recommended settings: l = m = 6, 8-10 triangulation rows (8n^2 facets), and phase function starting values a = 0.5, d = 0.1, k = -0.5, c = 0.1. The manual warns that fitting phase parameters with only relative data diverges.
results.source: DAMIT source package version_0.2.1.tar.gz from damit.cuni.cz/projects/damit/pages/software_download, file convexinv_doc.pdf (doc header reads 'version 0, June 2006'); local copy: C:\Users\kn18001\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-kn18001-Documents\98a1f892-0efb-441d-a311-b800785b2496\scratchpad\fc\damit\version_0.2.1\convexinv_doc.pdf
results.evidence: Manual p. 1: the first line of the input gives the number of lightcurves. Each block starts with the number of points and a 0 (relative) or 1 (calibrated) code. Each line holds a light-time-corrected JD, brightness in intensity units (reduced to unit Sun/Earth distances when calibrated), and the astrocentric ecliptic xyz of the Sun and Earth in AU. p. 2: l = m = 6 is a good choice, giving (l+1)^2 shape parameters, or (l+1)^2 - 1 for relative data. Triangulation uses typically 8-10 rows per octant, giving 8n^2 facets. Suggested start: a = 0.5, d = 0.1, k = -0.5, with c fixed at about 0.1. With relative data only, fix the phase parameters at zero amplitude and slope; fitting them leads to divergence. Note: the PDF calls itself version 0 (June 2006), although it ships in the v0.2.1 package.

results.claim: DAMIT manual: keep the dark facet below 1% of the total area by increasing the convexity regularization (typical 0.1, possibly orders of magnitude different). If a good fit is only possible with a large dark facet, albedo variegation is likely. period_scan reports the dark facet area in percent for each trial period.
results.source: DAMIT convexinv_doc.pdf (in version_0.2.1.tar.gz), pp. 2-4
results.evidence: p. 2: the convexity regularization weight is typically 0.1 but may need to be orders of magnitude larger or smaller. Keep the dark facet below 1% of the total area by increasing it. If a good fit needs a large dark facet, an albedo variation is likely. p. 3: the dark facet is written as facet 8n^2 + 1 and does not contribute photometrically. p. 4: the period_scan output file lists period, rms, chi2, iteration count and dark facet area (%) for each trial period.

results.claim: DAMIT period_scan: DeltaP is about 0.5 P^2/Deltat; the scan step is p DeltaP with p < 1 (recommended 0.8); number of trial periods = 2 Deltat (P1 - P0)/(P0 P1)/p. It uses six initial poles per trial period. Uniqueness in the manual is only qualitative: one pole significantly better than all others, and 5-10 random initial poles for convexinv.
results.source: DAMIT convexinv_doc.pdf (in version_0.2.1.tar.gz), p. 4; source file convexinv/period_scan.c
results.evidence: p. 4: DeltaP is about 0.5 P^2/Deltat, where Deltat is the full epoch range. The step is p DeltaP, with p always below 1 and 0.8 recommended. Nper = 2 Deltat (P1 - P0)/(P0 P1) times 1/p. period_scan starts from six initial poles per trial period, which the source period_scan.c also states ('six initial poles'). After the scan, run convexinv from five to ten random initial poles. A unique solution exists if only one pole gives significantly lower chi2, with the lambda+-180 mirror always possible. No numeric threshold is given.

findings.claim: MacLennan et al. ran both triaxial-ellipsoid and convex inversions, with MCMC uncertainties, on Gaia DR3 sparse photometry of more than 8000 asteroids. For most objects the ellipsoid pole matched the convex pole. They rejected 15% of the convex shapes, and they conclude that an ellipsoid is enough to estimate pole longitude and latitude from sparse data. Only the abstract was readable: the A&A full text returned HTTP 403, so the per-object pole differences were not seen.
findings.source: MacLennan, Pentikainen, Uvarova, Muinonen, Penttila, Wilawer, Oszkiewicz, Cellino, Tanga, Wang, Virkki 2026, A&A 707, A131 (volume/article number from search index); DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/202556031 (no arXiv id found)
findings.quote: for the vast majority of our objects the best-fit ellipsoid spin poles are comparable to that of a convex shape

findings.claim: The same paper's abstract states the conclusion directly. The authors fitted shape, spin and a linear phase slope with both shape families. Afterwards they derived H,G12 and H,G1,G2 from the predicted brightnesses.
findings.quote: The assumption of ellipsoid shape for sparse datasets is sufficient for estimating the spin pole longitude and latitude.

findings.claim: Durech & Hanus (Gaia DR3) built periodograms with two models. The first was a geometrically scattering triaxial ellipsoid with 2 shape parameters (a, b, with c=1). The second was a convex model with spherical harmonics of degree and order 3 (288 facets, 15 optimized shape coefficients). Lambert plus Lommel-Seeliger scattering was used, with only the linear phase term k free. Convex periodograms gave 6269 unique periods and ellipsoid periodograms gave 16010. Of the 3431 asteroids with periods from both, only 20 disagreed. Ellipsoids ran about 100 times faster. Final poles came from convex models refit at the ellipsoid periods, giving 8596 final models.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24; arXiv:2305.10798
findings.quote: we had a period solution from convex shape models and ellipsoids. Among them we found 20 asteroids for which the periods were different

findings.claim: Durech & Hanus name the case where an ellipsoid fails: lightcurves that are not double-sinusoidal (asymmetric or irregular). They chose ellipsoids for speed and for having fewer parameters than convex models.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24; arXiv:2305.10798
findings.quote: ellipsoidal shape models are insufficient when an asteroid's light curve significantly differs from a simple double sinusoidal curve

findings.claim: For (43) Ariadne the authors rebuilt DR3 models from different numbers of points and different spherical-harmonic resolutions. The poles scattered by only +/-2 deg in beta and +/-3 deg in lambda, but the shapes were not stable. Their uniqueness rule: the best chi2_min must be unique, with every other period above chi2_tr = (1 + sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min. They also required all ten jackknife subsets to return the same period.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24; arXiv:2305.10798 (Sect. 2.6, Fig. 3)
findings.quote: While spins derived from DR3 are reliable and stable with respect to the perturbations of input data

findings.claim: Gaia DR2 inversion used two models. The geometric ellipsoid has p = 6 parameters: P, lambda, beta, a linear phase slope, a/c and b/c. The degree-3 convex model has p = 20, of which 16 are shape parameters. Convex shapes can produce false half-period solutions, because they allow lightcurves with one maximum per rotation. Ellipsoids avoid this, but their periods are often wrong when N is small.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91; arXiv:1810.04485
findings.quote: Ellipsoidal models do not have this disadvantage of producing false half periods, but the periods based on a small number of points are often wrong.

findings.claim: Gaia DR2 convex models (about 5400 asteroids processed, 173 models) were checked against DAMIT. Periods agreed and the mean pole difference was 20 deg. Seven cases differed by more than 60 deg, which the authors attribute to different local minima. Periods were correct for more than half of the asteroids only when N > 30. The authors warn that DR2 convex shapes are not real shapes.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91; arXiv:1810.04485
findings.quote: the mean difference between their pole directions was 20°

findings.category: ellipsoid as period finder for convexinv
findings.claim: With Lowell sparse photometry (0.10-0.20 mag accuracy, similar to the MPC data here), a geometric triaxial ellipsoid was used to search for the period. Its period then seeded the final convex inversion. The ellipsoid often found the unique correct period when the convex scan gave many equally good minima.
findings.source: Durech, Hanus, Oszkiewicz, Vanco 2016, A&A 587, A48; arXiv:1601.02909
findings.quote: In many cases when the convex models gives many equally good solutions with different periods, this method provides a unique and correct rotation period.

findings.claim: Lowell sparse convex models were compared with 279 DAMIT models: 275 had the same period. The mean pole difference was 15 deg and the median 13 deg, which the authors read as the typical pole error from sparse data. False positives were estimated at a few percent. For 56 asteroids also modeled by Hanus et al. 2016, poles differed by 10-20 deg on average.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2016, A&A 587, A48; arXiv:1601.02909
findings.quote: the mean value is 15° and the median 13°

findings.category: ellipsoid model on apparition amplitudes/means (closest analogue to our method)
findings.claim: Cibulkova et al. used geometric triaxial ellipsoids fitted to the mean brightness and brightness dispersion per apparition, with free parameters lambda, beta, a/b and b/c and no period. This is nearly the same as our method. It returns lambda only modulo 180 deg and only |beta|, and beta was biased toward high values. Against 765 DAMIT models, a/b correlated at Pearson 0.48 (0.88 on synthetic data) and b/c was essentially undetermined (correlation < 0.1). They used it for population distributions, not individual models.
findings.source: Cibulkova, Durech, Vokrouhlicky, Kaasalainen, Oszkiewicz 2016, A&A 596, A57; arXiv:1610.02790
findings.quote: for most asteroids their sparse data are not accurate enough to derive a unique model and the lightcurve inversion method is thus not very efficient

findings.category: aspect-dependent mean-brightness model vs lightcurve-inversion poles
findings.claim: Carry et al.'s sHG1G2 model fits only aspect-dependent mean brightness: H, G1 and G2 per filter, plus spin (alpha0, delta0) and an oblateness R, for 3(Nf+1) parameters and no period. On ZTF data it was compared with literature spins for 6499 asteroids, mostly from lightcurve inversion (DAMIT). The angular differences peak at about 20 deg, with a median below 35 deg, and about 60% agree within 1 sigma. The conclusion summarizes agreement as typically 20-30 deg. The model cannot separate prograde from retrograde rotation, and R is biased low when the aspect coverage is narrow.
findings.source: Carry, Peloton, Le Montagner, Mahlke, Berthier 2024, A&A 687, A38; arXiv:2403.20179; DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/202449789
findings.quote: The distribution peaks around 20°, with half of the SSOs agreeing below 35°.

findings.claim: Takacs et al. fitted TESS-only data for 44 main-belt asteroids with a Lommel-Seeliger ellipsoid: one elongation parameter x (a=1+x, b=1, c=1-x) plus the pole. Their poles differed from DAMIT convex poles by about 33 deg on average and from the Gaia DR3 ellipsoid poles of Cellino et al. 2024 by about 25 deg. For 9 of 12 asteroids they were closer to Cellino 2024 than to DAMIT. They also report that Cellino 2024 ellipsoid poles differ from DAMIT convex poles by about 24 deg on average.
findings.source: Takacs, Kiss, Szakats, Pal 2025, PASP (accepted); arXiv:2503.13332
findings.quote: the average angular distance between the C24 and DAMIT pole solutions is ∼24°

findings.claim: Takacs et al. conclude that low-degree-of-freedom ellipsoid models are efficient for large surveys, but TESS-only geometry (few orbital positions) is often not enough to pin down the pole. Covering many orbital positions constrains the pole better than higher accuracy from fewer positions.
findings.source: Takacs et al. 2025, PASP; arXiv:2503.13332
findings.quote: These results highlight the limitations of low-degree-of-freedom models in asteroid light curve inversion.

findings.category: ellipsoid inversion validated on convex truth shapes (simulation)
findings.claim: Carbognani et al. simulated Gaia sparse photometry from 8 DAMIT convex shapes, using geometric scattering and no noise, then inverted it with the Gaia genetic triaxial-ellipsoid algorithm. Periods came out right except for (3) Juno (doubled). Poles agreed within delta-lambda = 2 +/- 1 deg and delta-beta = 3 +/- 8 deg, except a 180 deg longitude flip for (584) Semiramis. Volume errors were about 10% (at most 16%). The authors note that ellipsoids often cannot reproduce individual lightcurve details. Because the same scattering law was used to simulate and invert, with no noise, this is an optimistic test.
findings.source: Carbognani, Tanga, Cellino, Delbo, Mottola, Marchese 2012, Planet. Space Sci. 73, 80-85; arXiv:1903.12633; DOI 10.1016/j.pss.2011.12.002
findings.quote: between the genetic inversion and the complex or best-ellipsoidal models are ∆λ = 2 ± 1° and ∆β = 3 ± 8°

findings.claim: Carbognani et al. conclude that the ellipsoid assumption does not seriously bias period or spin. They add that ellipsoids often fail to reproduce single lightcurves, and that individual cases with large discrepancies still need to be identified.
findings.source: Carbognani et al. 2012, PSS 73, 80; arXiv:1903.12633
findings.quote: although unable - in many cases - to reproduce the details of single light curves

findings.category: ellipsoid inversion of nonconvex simulated objects
findings.claim: Santana-Ros et al. tested the Gaia genetic ellipsoid inversion on 10,359 nonconvex Gaussian-sphere shapes (Z-buffer brightness, sigma = 0.03 mag). 65% of solutions were accepted, and 83% of those were correct. On an ellipsoid control sample, more than 99% of poles were recovered within 5 deg. There was no direct comparison with convex inversion.
findings.source: Santana-Ros, Bartczak, Michalowski, Tanga, Cellino 2015, MNRAS 450, 333-341; arXiv:1504.02809; DOI 10.1093/mnras/stv631
findings.quote: accepted by the inversion software and the correct solution was found for 83 per cent of them

findings.category: failure modes for sparse ellipsoid inversion
findings.claim: The worst cases were quasi-spherical shapes (about 30% wrong on average), low pole latitudes (|beta| < 30 deg) and fewer than 50 points. Adding a single dense lightcurve reduced the number of wrong solutions.
findings.source: Santana-Ros et al. 2015, MNRAS 450, 333; arXiv:1504.02809
findings.quote: asteroids having quasi-spherical shape, low pole latitudes and less than 50 data points

findings.claim: Cellino et al. 2019 inverted Gaia DR2 and Hipparcos data with a Lommel-Seeliger triaxial ellipsoid. The more flexible cellinoid shape (8 ellipsoid octants, 3 extra parameters) determined the spin period better. Fewer than 30 points were often enough for a period, but DR2 left the pole direction uncertain. Only the abstract was readable (A&A full text: HTTP 403).
findings.source: Cellino, Hestroffer, Lu, Muinonen, Tanga 2019, A&A 631, A67; DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201936059 (no arXiv version found)
findings.quote: Using the more realistic cellinoid shape model, we find further improvement in the determination of the spin period.

findings.claim: Cellino et al. 2024 ran the Gaia DPAC genetic ellipsoid inversion on 22,815 DR3 asteroids, mostly with 40 points or fewer. About 85% of periods were correct against reliable literature values after filtering. Multiple equivalent period solutions were not systematically examined. Only the abstract was readable.
findings.source: Cellino, Tanga, Muinonen, Mignard 2024, A&A (Asteroid spin and shape properties from Gaia DR3 photometry); DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/202449297
findings.quote: the algorithm was set to adopt a simple triaxial ellipsoid shape model

findings.category: ellipsoid vs convex in a controlled simulation
findings.claim: Muinonen et al. 2022 simulated a Gaussian-sphere asteroid: 29 dense lightcurves plus 39 sparse points, 0.01 mag noise. Convex MCMC recovered the pole as (24.63 +/- 0.59, 62.9 +/- 1.3) deg against the true (25.018, 62.89) deg. The ellipsoid model (9 parameters) gave (28.5 +/- 1.5, 58.0 +/- 3.7) deg for absolute photometry, about 5 deg off by my calculation, and (23.9, 60.5) deg for relative photometry. The authors still judge ellipsoid inversion acceptable. Even the convex fit could not reach the simulated noise level, because the phase-function and scattering model were too restrictive.
findings.source: Muinonen, Uvarova, Martikainen, Penttila, Cellino, Wang 2022, Front. Astron. Space Sci. 9, 821125; DOI 10.3389/fspas.2022.821125
findings.quote: With ellipsoids, there can be statistically significant differences from the true values of the parameters.

findings.claim: Muinonen et al. 2020 built MCMC convex inversion and applied it to Gaia DR2 data for (21) Lutetia, (26) Proserpina and (585) Bilkis. They used Gaia-only triaxial-ellipsoid inversion mainly to show that Gaia photometry yields meaningful phase slopes. Ellipsoid inversion needed a modified observational uncertainty model. Only the abstract was readable.
findings.source: Muinonen, Torppa, Wang, Cellino, Penttila 2020, A&A 642, A138; DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/202038036
findings.quote: For inverse methods involving triaxial ellipsoids, we update the uncertainty model for the observations.

findings.claim: Muinonen et al. 2015 present the Lommel-Seeliger ellipsoid, which has an analytic disk-integrated brightness, as a fast initial estimate of period, pole and shape (including MCMC) for sparse and dense data. It is meant to come before more detailed modeling (abstract only).
findings.source: Muinonen, Wilkman, Cellino, Wang, Wang 2015, Planet. Space Sci. 118, 227-241; DOI 10.1016/j.pss.2015.09.005
findings.quote: in a majority of cases, initial LS ellipsoid retrieval of the parameters is satisfactory

findings.category: review: ellipsoid adequacy for sparse data
findings.claim: The Asteroids IV review states that a triaxial ellipsoid is usually enough for noisy sparse data. It cites Cellino et al. 2009, Cellino & Dell'Oro 2012 and Carbognani et al. 2012, and notes that only two shape parameters make period scanning fast. It also says pole accuracy ranges from a few degrees with many dense lightcurves to more than 20 deg for limited, noisy data.
findings.source: Durech, Carry, Delbo, Kaasalainen, Viikinkoski 2015, Asteroids IV, 183-202; arXiv:1502.04816
findings.quote: a simple shape model of a triaxial ellipsoid is usually sufficient to model the data and to derive the correct period and spin vector orientation

findings.category: review: what sparse data can constrain
findings.claim: Kaasalainen & Durech say sparse photometry can give period and spin but only a crude shape. The spin direction is not affected by the shape/albedo ambiguity. With calibrated sparse data the phase curve must be fitted, for example with the exponential-linear phase function times Lommel-Seeliger plus Lambert scattering used in convexinv. They also note that prograde/retrograde ambiguity comes from insufficient data, not from the lambda+180 symmetry.
findings.source: Kaasalainen & Durech 2020, arXiv:2005.09947 (Asteroid models from generalised projections)
findings.quote: successful inversion (though obviously crude for shape) can be carried out for very sparse photometry

findings.claim: Kaasalainen & Durech recommend gradient-based Levenberg-Marquardt optimization started from many initial values, as in convexinv. They call genetic algorithms poor for this problem because they lose track of other acceptable minima. They also warn against inverse crime: simulating data with the same model used to invert it gives overconfident results.
findings.source: Kaasalainen & Durech 2020, arXiv:2005.09947
findings.quote: Genetic algorithms are a particularly poor variation of these for this problem

findings.category: convex resolution sensitivity with 0.1-mag survey data
findings.claim: Hanus & Durech ran convex inversion on Catalina (703) sparse data alone, with magnitudes given to 0.1 mag (about 12% accuracy), at resolutions n = 2 to 6. The period was stable across resolutions, but pole longitude often moved by 50 deg or more. They recommend accepting a model only if a rerun at n=3 (period step 0.5 dP) gives a similar unique solution. 7 of 13 CSS-only models agreed well with reference models.
findings.source: Hanus & Durech 2012, Planet. Space Sci. 73, 75-79; arXiv:1301.7205; DOI 10.1016/j.pss.2012.01.014
findings.quote: The dispersion in the ecliptic latitude of the pole direction was usually ≲20°, but in the ecliptic longitude of the pole direction often ≳50°.

findings.category: MPC/AstDyS sparse data handling for convexinv
findings.claim: Hanus et al. 2011 used AstDyS/MPC sparse photometry from 689, 699, 703, E12, G96, 950 and Hipparcos. They weighted it against dense data (weight 1): USNO 0.3, Hipparcos 0.3, Catalina 0.15, La Palma 0.15, LONEOS 0.1, Siding Spring 0.1, Mt Lemmon 0.1. They excluded observatories with large scatter and estimated pole uncertainty at +/-10-20 deg. For 16 asteroids, sparse-only models matched DAMIT models built from independent data.
findings.source: Hanus, Durech, Broz et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134; arXiv:1104.4114
findings.quote: Observatories with a high median or 'FWHM' value (≳0.2 mag for both) are not suitable for the lightcurve inversion.

findings.claim: Santana-Ros et al. 2017 say the DPAC chose ellipsoids because about 60-70 Gaia points per object cannot constrain a complex shape alone. Convex shapes from sparse data are usually low-resolution and angular.
findings.source: Santana-Ros, Dudzinski, Bartczak 2017, Astrophys. Space Sci. Proc. 46 (Assessment and Mitigation of Asteroid Impact Hazards); arXiv:1705.05710
findings.quote: this number of measurements is not enough to constrain a complex model shape by its own

findings.category: crude ellipsoid model: population vs individual
findings.claim: Nortunen et al. tested an ellipsoid brightness-variation model on DAMIT-based synthetic populations. It is robust only for population distributions of elongation and spin latitude, not for individual objects. Local shape irregularities shift the inferred elongation even without noise.
findings.source: Nortunen, Kaasalainen, Durech, Cibulkova, Ali-Lagoa, Hanus 2017, A&A 601, A139; arXiv:1703.07178
findings.quote: The large number of brightness variation samples, rather than the accuracy of the observable, is the main reason why the method can tolerate the crude underlying shape model.

findings.claim: For (103) Hera, on the same mostly dense ground-based data, convex inversion gave poles (83.0, 39.0) and (269.7, 56.8) deg. The Lommel-Seeliger ellipsoid gave (74.1, 39.0) and (263.1, 51.0) deg, with the same period to about 1e-4 h. By my calculation the angular differences are about 7 deg.
findings.source: Wang, Wang, Muinonen, Han 2019, Planet. Space Sci. 167, 17-22; DOI 10.1016/j.pss.2019.01.007
findings.quote: a pair of pole solutions – ( 74 . 1 °, 39 . 0 °) and ( 263 . 1 °, 51 . 0 °) with a spin period of 23.74262 h

findings.category: convex inversion on combined survey photometry (MPC-type data)
findings.claim: A 2025 conference abstract by Durech & Hanus reports the Prague pipeline on combined Catalina, Mt Lemmon, Pan-STARRS, ZTF, ATLAS, TESS, ASAS-SN, USNO and Gaia DR3 photometry. They obtained models for about 23,000 of about 330,000 asteroids. This is the same kind of multi-observatory data we have.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2025, EPSC-DPS2025-96 (conference abstract)
findings.quote: hundreds of data points per asteroid

findings.claim: DAMIT software v0.2.1 is Durech's C translation of Kaasalainen's Fortran. convexinv optimizes all parameters using a spherical-harmonics shape; conjgradinv polishes only the facet areas at the end. Lightcurve files flag each lightcurve as relative (0) or calibrated (1), and the scattering model is Lambert plus Lommel-Seeliger.
findings.source: DAMIT software download and documentation pages (Astronomical Institute, Charles University); method refs Kaasalainen & Torppa 2001 Icarus 153, 24; Kaasalainen, Torppa & Muinonen 2001 Icarus 153, 37
findings.quote: optimizes all parameters and uses spherical harmonics functions for shape representation

research.notes:
WHAT THE LITERATURE SAYS ABOUT ELLIPSOID VS CONVEX FOR SPARSE DATA
1. Poles: for sparse data, ellipsoid and convex models agree for most objects.
   - MacLennan et al. 2026 (Gaia DR3, about 8000 objects) found the poles comparable and concluded that an ellipsoid is enough for the pole.
   - Durech & Hanus 2023: of 3431 asteroids with periods from both models, only 20 disagreed.
   - Takacs et al. 2025 report that Cellino 2024 ellipsoid poles differ from DAMIT convex poles by about 24 deg on average.
   - No paper I read shows that convex shapes give significantly better poles from sparse data alone.
2. Typical pole error from sparse data, whatever the model, is 10-30 deg:
   - Lowell vs DAMIT: mean 15, median 13 deg (Durech 2016).
   - Gaia DR2 vs DAMIT: mean 20 deg (Durech & Hanus 2018).
   - sHG1G2 vs literature: peak about 20 deg, median below 35 deg (Carry 2024).
   - Asteroids IV review: more than 20 deg for limited, noisy data.
   - Hanus 2011: +/-10-20 deg.
   - So pole differences of about 15-25 deg between our ellipsoid fit and convexinv are expected scatter, not proof that either is better. Also watch for lambda vs lambda+180 swaps.
3. Strengths of each model:
   - Ellipsoids (p=6) never give false half periods, run about 100 times faster, and often find the unique period when the convex scan gives many minima (Durech 2016, 2018). The Prague group uses ellipsoids to find the period, then convex for the final model.
   - Convex models (degree 3: p=20) are needed when lightcurves are not double-sinusoidal (Durech & Hanus 2023). A flexible shape (cellinoid) improved Gaia period recovery (Cellino 2019).
   - In a controlled simulation that included dense data, convex poles were closer to the truth: about 0.5 deg vs about 5 deg (Muinonen 2022).
4. When convex is justified for sparse data, per the authors:
   - enough points (more than about 30 for Gaia-quality data; more than about 100 calibrated points over 3-5 yr at about 5% accuracy, per Hanus 2011);
   - several apparitions;
   - a solution that stays the same when re-run at lower resolution (Hanus & Durech 2012: rerun at n=3) and under jackknife subsets (Durech & Hanus 2023);
   - a period that passes the uniqueness test chi2_tr = (1 + sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min.
   - Sparse convex shapes should not be read as real shapes.
   - With 0.1-mag, CSS-like data the pole longitude can shift by 50 deg or more between resolutions. Expect this for our quantized 703/G96-type sets.
5. Our per-apparition amplitude/mean ellipsoid method is closest to Cibulkova et al. 2016 and Carry et al. 2024 (sHG1G2). Those methods have no period, give lambda only modulo 180 deg and only |beta|, and bias beta high. Their authors present them mainly for population statistics, not individual models.

SUGGESTIONS FOR OUR COMPARISON (my inference, not from the papers)
- Compare the two fits on the same observable. convexinv fits individual points, so either:
  - fit the ellipsoid to the individual points as well (as in the Durech & Hanus ellipsoid periodogram), or
  - compute per-apparition amplitudes and means from the convexinv model.
- Judge improvement with chi2 against degrees of freedom (nu = N - p, with p about 20 vs 6), using the chi2_tr criterion or an F-test. A lower raw RMS alone does not show improvement.
- Weight observatories as Hanus 2011 did (0.1-0.3 relative to dense data) and drop high-scatter stations.
