results.claim: MacLennan et al. ran ellipsoid and convex inversions with MCMC on Gaia DR3 sparse photometry of more than 8000 asteroids. For most objects the ellipsoid pole matched the convex pole. They rejected 15% of convex shapes and conclude an ellipsoid is enough for pole lambda and beta. Only the abstract was readable (A&A full text 403).
results.evidence: Full abstract read from the Crossref record (api.crossref.org/works/10.1051/0004-6361/202556031), raw JATS text. Title: 'Asteroid characterization using Gaia Data Release 3. I. Shapes, spins, and scattering properties'. Vol 707, A131, March 2026; the 11 authors are as listed. The abstract says 'over 8000 asteroids based solely on DR3 photometry', triaxial ellipsoid and convex shapes, and 'Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling'. It contains 'We rejected 15% of convex shapes' and the quoted sentence on ellipsoid vs convex poles, verbatim. The aanda.org full_html, abs and pdf pages all returned HTTP 403 to me too, so I saw no per-object pole differences. No arXiv version found.

results.claim: The abstract states the conclusion directly. They fitted shape, spin and linear phase slope with both shape families, then derived H,G12 and H,G1,G2 from predicted brightnesses.
results.evidence: Crossref abstract, Methods section: 'we sought the best-fit shape, spin, and linear slope, along with their uncertainties, via a Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling technique'. Also: 'We also fit H, G12 and H, G1, G2 phase functions from predicted brightnesses derived from the fit shapes.' The Conclusions sentence on the ellipsoid assumption appears verbatim. The abstract also reports no correlation between family shapes/spins and family ages.

results.claim: Durech & Hanus (DR3): ellipsoid with 2 shape params (a,b; c=1); convex SH degree/order 3, 288 facets, 15 coefficients; Lambert+LS with only k free. Convex periodograms gave 6269 unique periods, ellipsoid periodograms 16010. Of 3431 with both, 20 disagreed. Ellipsoids about 100x faster. Final poles from convex refits at the ellipsoid periods, 8596 final models.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24; arXiv:2305.10798
results.corrected_claim: Model settings are correct: the ellipsoid has 2 shape parameters (a, b, shortest axis = 1) with geometric scattering. The convex model uses spherical harmonics of degree and order 3, 288 surface elements and 15 optimized coefficients. Scattering is Lambert + Lommel-Seeliger, with only the linear phase term k optimized (a0=0.5, d=0.1 fixed). Ellipsoids are about 100x faster. The counts were mixed across stages. Convex-shape periodograms gave 14,192 asteroids with a unique period. A pole search cut that to 11,854, and after all selection criteria 6269 convex-based models were left. Ellipsoid periodograms gave 16,010 unique periods. Convex models were then fitted at those periods and the same selection applied, leaving 5784 models. Of the 3431 asteroids in both sets, 20 had different periods. The final set is 8602 reliable models, minus 6 rejected by comparison with LCDB/DAMIT, giving 8596. That set is the union of both routes, so convex refits at ellipsoid periods supply only part of the final poles.
results.evidence: ar5iv 2305.10798: 'We obtained a sample of 14,192 asteroids with a unique period defined this way' (convex SH 3,3 search, 288 surface elements). 'The analysis of ellipsoid-based periodograms resulted in 16,010 unique periods. After finding the unique period, we modeled the data with the standard convex shape approximation'. 'we obtained a set of 6269 models based on a convex-shape period search and 5784 models based on a period search with ellipsoids.' 'For 3431 asteroids, we had a period solution from convex shape models and ellipsoids. Among them we found 20 asteroids for which the periods were different.' 'Out of the 8602 asteroids that passed all the checks ... 6 were excluded ... so there are 8596 final models.' Speed: 'about a hundred times faster than when using convex shapes'. Phase: 'we optimized only the linear parameter k'.

results.claim: Durech & Hanus say an ellipsoid fails when lightcurves are not double-sinusoidal, and chose ellipsoids for speed and fewer parameters.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24; arXiv:2305.10798
results.evidence: ar5iv: 'However, ellipsoidal shape models are insufficient when an asteroid's light curve significantly differs from a simple double sinusoidal curve.' The stated advantage is that 'the number of model parameters is smaller than in the case of convex models (only two parameters describing the shape...)', 'about a hundred times faster'. They also say rotation about the shortest axis is physically correct. 'Asymmetric or irregular' is the claimant's own wording, not the paper's.

results.claim: (43) Ariadne rebuilt from different point numbers and SH resolutions; poles scattered +/-2 deg in beta and +/-3 deg in lambda, shapes not stable. Uniqueness: chi2_tr=(1+sqrt(2/nu))chi2_min. All ten jackknife subsets had to return the same period.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24; arXiv:2305.10798 (Sect. 2.6, Fig. 3)
results.corrected_claim: The Ariadne part is correct. Fig. 3 uses 20, 30, 40 and 53 points and resolutions from 3,3 to 5,5. Pole dispersion is +/-2 deg in beta and +/-3 deg in lambda, and the shape models are not stable. The chi2_tr uniqueness rule is correct. The jackknife rule is looser than stated. The data are split into ten parts and one part (~10%) is removed per run. An asteroid is kept if all ten jackknife periods match the original within 0.1%, or if at most one disagrees (i.e. nine of ten match).
results.evidence: ar5iv: 'selected only asteroids for which all ten jackknife periods were the same (within 0.1%) as the original period or for which there was at most one disagreement'. 'the dispersion in spin directions for different shape models in Fig. 3 is ±2° in ecliptic latitude β and ±3° in ecliptic longitude λ), the shape models are not'. Fig. 3 caption: 'reconstructed from different numbers of data points and with different degrees and orders of spherical harmonics'. Uniqueness: 'lowest χ²_min with all other periods giving χ² higher than χ²_tr=(1+√(2/ν))χ²_min'.

results.claim: Gaia DR2: ellipsoid p=6 (P, lambda, beta, linear phase slope, a/c, b/c); degree-3 convex p=20 with 16 shape params. Convex gives false half periods (one maximum per rotation); ellipsoids avoid this but small-N periods are often wrong.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91; arXiv:1810.04485
results.evidence: ar5iv 1810.04485: 'For ellipsoids, p=6 and the parameters are the sidereal rotation period P, the spin axis direction ... λ and β, one parameter for the linear slope of the phase curve, and two parameters (a/c and b/c)'. Convex: 'order and degree of three, which corresponds to 16 shape parameters, so the total number of parameters is p=20.' Half periods: 'this can happen with convex shapes as they produce lightcurves with only one minimum/maximum per rotation.' The quoted sentence about ellipsoids is verbatim.

results.claim: DR2 convex models (~5400 processed, 173 models) vs DAMIT: periods agreed, mean pole difference 20 deg. Seven cases >60 deg, attributed to different local minima. Periods correct for >half only when N>30. DR2 convex shapes are not real shapes.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91; arXiv:1810.04485
results.corrected_claim: About 5400 asteroids with at least ten DR2 points were processed, giving 173 models (129 new). Most agreed with DAMIT: same period within errors and a mean pole difference of 20 deg. Seven outliers had pole differences >60 deg, for three different reasons. In one, (2802) Weisell, the DAMIT sparse-only model was wrong (wrong local minimum) and was removed from DAMIT. In five, the periods were very similar and the DR2 solution was apparently a different local minimum with a different pole. In one, the periods were completely different. The fraction of periods matching LCDB within +/-5% rises above 0.5 only when N>30; this holds for ellipsoid and convex results combined. The authors warn that DR2 convex shapes are not real shapes.
results.evidence: ar5iv: 'By processing about 5400 asteroids with at least ten observations in DR2, we derived models for 173 asteroids, 129 of which are new.' The 20° mean pole difference quote is verbatim. On the outliers: '(2802) Weisell – the DAMIT model ... was clearly incorrect'; 'In five cases ... apparently a different local minimum leading to a different pole. In one case, the periods were completely different.' 'The fraction of correctly determined periods (... agree with LCDB values within ±5%) increases above 0.5 when N>30.' 'Convex shape models derived from DR2 data should not be taken as real shapes'.

results.claim: Lowell sparse photometry (0.10-0.20 mag): geometric triaxial ellipsoid used for period search, its period seeded convex inversion; ellipsoid often found the unique correct period when convex gave many equally good minima.
results.source: Durech, Hanus, Oszkiewicz, Vanco 2016, A&A 587, A48; arXiv:1601.02909
results.evidence: ar5iv 1601.02909: 'The accuracy of the data is around 0.10–0.20 mag.' The ellipsoid uses a geometrical scattering model for which the brightness can be computed analytically. Its significant chi2 minimum in period serves as the start for convex inversion. The quoted sentence ('In many cases when the convex models gives many equally good solutions...') is verbatim.

results.claim: Lowell convex models vs 279 DAMIT models: 275 same period; mean pole difference 15 deg, median 13 deg (typical pole error); false positives a few percent; 56 asteroids also in Hanus et al. 2016 differ by 10-20 deg on average.
results.source: Durech et al. 2016, A&A 587, A48; arXiv:1601.02909

'the mean value is 15° and the median 13°' is called 'a typical error in the pole determination that was based on Lowell data'. False positives: 'around a few percent'. On the 56 Hanus et al. 2016 asteroids: 'pole directions differ by 10–20 degrees on average'.

results.claim: Cibulkova et al.: geometric triaxial ellipsoids fit to mean brightness and dispersion per apparition; free lambda, beta, a/b, b/c, no period; lambda mod 180 and |beta|; beta biased high; vs 765 DAMIT models a/b Pearson 0.48 (0.88 synthetic), b/c <0.1; used for population distributions.

Lambda is known only modulo 180° and only |beta|. 'The determination of ecliptical latitudes β shows bias towards finding preferentially spin axes near the ecliptic pole.' 'We compared resulting ratios a/b and b/c of 765 asteroids included in DAMIT'. Table 1, Pearson: a/b 0.48 real vs 0.88 synthetic; b/c 0.053 real vs 0.35 synthetic. The quoted sentence on sparse data accuracy is verbatim.

results.claim: Carry et al. sHG1G2: H,G1,G2 per filter + alpha0, delta0, R; 3(Nf+1) params, no period. Vs literature spins for 6499 asteroids (mostly lightcurve inversion/DAMIT): peak ~20 deg, median below 35 deg, ~60% within 1 sigma; conclusion 20-30 deg; cannot separate prograde/retrograde; R biased low with narrow aspect coverage.
results.source: Carry, Peloton, Le Montagner, Mahlke, Berthier 2024, A&A 687, A38; arXiv:2403.20179
results.corrected_claim: Everything is correct except the median. The paper says half of the SSOs agree below 35 deg, so the median angular difference is about 35 deg, not below 35 deg. The rest checks out: 3x(Nf+1) parameters, no period, 6,499 SSOs with literature spins (mainly lightcurve inversion, compiled in DAMIT), distribution peak around 20 deg, about 60% within 1 sigma (95% within 3 sigma), and a conclusion of 'typically 20–30°'. There is a complete degeneracy between the two rotation senses, and two solutions are reported: (alpha0, delta0) and (alpha0+180, -delta0). The low-R tail is called an artifact of a very limited aspect-angle range and/or obliquity near 0 or 180 deg.
results.evidence: The arXiv HTML and ar5iv pages were truncated before Sect. 4.5, so I extracted the text from the arXiv PDF locally. Sect. 4.5: 'We find 6,499 SSOs with previous estimates of the spin-axis coordinates, mainly from the lightcurve inversion technique'. The quoted sentence on the 20° peak and 35° is verbatim. 'About 60% of the solutions agree within one σ, and 95% at three σ'. Conclusions: 'agree with those determined with other methods ... within typically 20–30°'. 'complete degeneracy between direct and prograde rotation' (the paper's own wording). Sect. 4.6: the low-R tail 'is an artifact as most SSOs with an oblateness below 0.5 have observations covering a very limited range of aspect angle'. Sect. 3: 'for a total of 3×(Nf +1) parameters'.

results.claim: Takacs et al.: TESS-only, 44 main-belt asteroids, LS ellipsoid a=1+x, b=1, c=1-x plus pole; ~33 deg from DAMIT, ~25 deg from Cellino 2024; 9 of 12 closer to C24; C24 vs DAMIT ~24 deg.
results.source: Takacs, Kiss, Szakats, Pal 2025, PASP (accepted); arXiv:2503.13332
results.evidence: arXiv abstract: '44 selected main belt asteroids, using light curve inversion, assuming Lommel-Seeliger ellipsoids'; accepted in PASP. HTML: 'a=1+x, b=1 and c=1−x' with x from 0.0 to 0.5. DAMIT comparison: 'the average separation of ∼33°'. C24 comparison, 12 common objects: 'approximately ∼25°'. 'In most cases (9 out of 12), the distance between the C24 and our TESS results is lower'. The quoted sentence on the ~24° C24-DAMIT distance is verbatim.

results.claim: Takacs et al. conclude low-DOF ellipsoids are efficient for large surveys, but TESS-only geometry often cannot pin the pole; many orbital positions beat higher accuracy at fewer positions.
results.source: Takacs et al. 2025, PASP; arXiv:2503.13332
results.evidence: arXiv HTML conclusions, verbatim: 'These results highlight the limitations of low-degree-of-freedom models in asteroid light curve inversion. While such models allow for the efficient analysis of large survey datasets, ... TESS data alone are often insufficient for reliably reconstructing spin axis orientations.' Also: a dataset covering multiple orbital points 'provides better constraints ... than a dataset that samples fewer points but does so with more accuracy.' TESS gives at most 3-4 orbital phases.

results.claim: Carbognani et al.: 8 DAMIT convex shapes, geometric scattering, no noise, Gaia genetic ellipsoid inversion; periods right except (3) Juno doubled; dlambda=2+/-1, dbeta=3+/-8 deg, except 180 deg flip for (584) Semiramis; volume ~10% (max 16%); ellipsoids often miss lightcurve details; optimistic test.
results.source: Carbognani, Tanga, Cellino, Delbo, Mottola, Marchese 2012, PSS 73, 80-85; arXiv:1903.12633; DOI 10.1016/j.pss.2011.12.002
results.evidence: Text extracted from the arXiv PDF. Eight S-type MBAs: Juno, Herculina, Metis, Nausikaa, Semiramis, Pittsburghia, Mitaka, Datura; 'all having convex shapes' from DAMIT. Only geometric-scattering results are reported (the 10% Lambert + 90% LS runs were still in progress). 'we didn't study the effect of photometric noise'. Juno's period came out 'twice of the real value'. The quoted Δλ/Δβ values are verbatim; 'The only great exception is for the spin longitude of 584 Semiramis ... about 180°'. Volume errors 'not greater than 16%', 'usually around 10%'. Calling it 'optimistic' is the claimant's reading, but it is consistent with the setup.

results.claim: Carbognani et al. conclude the ellipsoid assumption does not seriously bias period or spin; ellipsoids often fail to reproduce single lightcurves; individual large-discrepancy cases need identifying.
results.source: Carbognani et al. 2012, PSS 73, 80; arXiv:1903.12633
results.evidence: Conclusions: genetic ellipsoids 'do not heavily affect the physical parameters that can be derived (rotation period, spin)'. The quoted clause about single light curves is verbatim. Then: 'research on individual cases is probably needed to identify those cases that can present remarkable discrepancies.'

results.claim: Santana-Ros et al. 2015: 10,359 nonconvex Gaussian-sphere shapes, Z-buffer, sigma=0.03; 65% accepted, 83% of those correct; ellipsoid control >99% poles within 5 deg; no direct comparison with convex inversion.
results.source: Santana-Ros, Bartczak, Michalowski, Tanga, Cellino 2015, MNRAS 450, 333; arXiv:1504.02809
results.evidence: Text extracted from the arXiv PDF. 'we generated a set of 10 359 random non-convex shapes using Gaussian spheres'; brightness from the 'Z-buffer standard graphic method'; noise 'σ = 0.03'. '65 per cent of the 10 359 asteroids were accepted ... correct solution was found for 83 per cent of them' (5632 correct, 1122 incorrect). Noiseless triaxial-ellipsoid control test: 'correct pole (within 5 degrees ...) ... for more than 99 per cent of inversion runs'. There is no convex-inversion comparison.

results.claim: Worst cases: quasi-spherical shapes (~30% wrong on average), low pole latitudes (|beta|<30 deg), fewer than 50 points. Adding a single dense lightcurve reduced wrong solutions.
results.source: Santana-Ros et al. 2015, MNRAS 450, 333; arXiv:1504.02809
results.corrected_claim: The three problem cases are confirmed: quasi-spherical shapes, low pole latitudes, and fewer than 50 data points. The ~30% wrong rate is for quasi-spherical bodies, especially those with low pole latitude, and half of that group's solutions were also refused with a warning flag. The paper gives no |beta|<30 deg threshold for 'low latitude' in the nonconvex test. That number comes from the noiseless ellipsoid control test, where most of the rare wrong periods had |beta|<30 deg. Adding one simulated 60-point lightcurve (sigma 0.03) helped little. The improvement was 'almost negligible' except for nearly spherical objects and asteroids with fewer than 50 Gaia detections. It worked by reducing accepted wrong solutions, not by adding correct ones.
results.evidence: Text extracted from the arXiv PDF. 'worst results are obtained for the quasi-spherical bodies and, in particular, for those having a low pole latitude ... (around 30 per cent on the average)'. Control test: 'majority of the wrong solutions are confined to pole latitudes with |β| < 30 degrees'. Sect. 4.1: 'with the exception of nearly spherical objects, the improvement was almost negligible'. Sect. 4.2: improvement 'clearly appreciated for asteroids having less than 50 detections'. Conclusions list the three problem scenarios and say adding a single lightcurve can reduce wrong solutions.

results.claim: Cellino et al. 2019: LS triaxial ellipsoid on Gaia DR2 and Hipparcos; cellinoid (8 ellipsoid octants, 3 extra parameters) improved period; <30 points often enough; DR2 pole uncertain; abstract only.
results.source: Cellino, Hestroffer, Lu, Muinonen, Tanga 2019, A&A 631, A67; DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/201936059
results.corrected_claim: From the abstract (via Crossref): the updated algorithm uses an LS scattering law for triaxial ellipsoids on GDR2 and older Hipparcos data. Hipparcos results improved only marginally, while the Gaia results were 'very encouraging'. The period could be found in most cases, but the short GDR2 time span leaves the spin axis direction uncertain. Fewer than 30 measurements were in many cases enough for a satisfactory inversion solution. The cellinoid model gave a further improvement in the spin period. The abstract does not describe the cellinoid as 8 ellipsoid octants with 3 extra parameters. That detail comes from elsewhere and could not be checked against this paper.
results.evidence: Crossref abstract: 'includes the treatment of a Lommel-Seeliger scattering relation especially developed for the case of triaxial ellipsoid shapes'; 'Even a small number of measurements, less than 30 in many cases, are sufficient to obtain a satisfactory inversion solution.' The quoted cellinoid sentence is verbatim. A&A 631, A67 (22 Oct 2019) confirmed. The abstract never mentions octants or a parameter count.

results.claim: Cellino et al. 2024: Gaia DPAC genetic ellipsoid inversion on 22,815 DR3 asteroids, mostly <=40 points; ~85% correct periods vs literature after filtering; multiple equivalent period solutions not systematically examined; abstract only.
results.source: Cellino, Tanga, Muinonen, Mignard 2024, A&A; DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/202449297
results.evidence: Crossref abstract: A&A 687, A277 (July 2024). 'a set of 22 815 objects'; 'the algorithm was set to adopt a simple triaxial ellipsoid shape model'. Points: 'in the majority of cases no greater than 40'. 'the proportion of correct determinations for the spin period ... is about 85%', after 'a moderate filtering procedure'. The abstract mentions 'multiple, equivalent spin period solutions that have not been systematically investigated'. The missing volume/article number is A&A 687, A277.

results.claim: Muinonen et al. 2022: Gaussian-sphere sim, 29 dense LCs + 39 sparse points, 0.01 mag; convex MCMC (24.63+/-0.59, 62.9+/-1.3) vs true (25.018, 62.89); 9-parameter ellipsoid (28.5+/-1.5, 58.0+/-3.7) absolute, ~5 deg off, (23.9, 60.5) relative; ellipsoid still acceptable; convex could not reach noise level due to restrictive phase function/scattering.
results.source: Muinonen, Uvarova, Martikainen, Penttila, Cellino, Wang 2022, Front. Astron. Space Sci. 9, 821125; DOI 10.3389/fspas.2022.821125
results.evidence: Frontiers full text: '29 dense lightcurves with altogether 6,664 data points and a single sparse lightcurve with 39 data points', Gaussian errors of 0.01 mag. Table 8: true 25.018/62.89; CXI absolute MCMC 24.63/62.9; EI absolute 28.5/58.0; EI relative 23.9/60.5 (±3.8/±4.0); CXI relative 24.80/62.5. Ellipsoid 'N_P = 9 free parameters' (P, λ, β, phase, two axial ratios, three phase-function parameters). Both the quoted sentence and 'ellipsoid inversion works in an acceptable way both for relative and absolute photometry' are present. 'Even with convex inversion, the goodness of fit cannot reach the standard deviation ... restrictive linear-exponential phase function and the pure Lommel-Seeliger scattering model.' My own calculation of the ellipsoid absolute offset is 5.2 deg.

results.claim: Muinonen et al. 2020: MCMC convex inversion on Gaia DR2 for Lutetia, Proserpina, Bilkis; Gaia-only ellipsoid inversion mainly to show meaningful phase slopes; ellipsoid needed modified uncertainty model; abstract only.
results.source: Muinonen, Torppa, Wang, Cellino, Penttila 2020, A&A 642, A138; DOI 10.1051/0004-6361/202038036
results.evidence: Crossref abstract: an MCMC sampler for general convex shapes, applied to (21) Lutetia, (26) Proserpina and (585) Bilkis with DR2. 'with the help of triaxial ellipsoid inversion as applied to Gaia photometry only, we provide additional proof that the absolute Gaia photometry alone can yield meaningful photometric slope parameters.' The quoted sentence on the uncertainty model is verbatim. A&A 642, A138 confirmed.

results.claim: Muinonen et al. 2015: LS ellipsoid with analytic disk-integrated brightness as fast initial estimate of period, pole, shape (incl. MCMC) for sparse and dense data, before more detailed modeling (abstract only).
results.source: Muinonen, Wilkman, Cellino, Wang, Wang 2015, PSS 118, 227; DOI 10.1016/j.pss.2015.09.005
results.evidence: Abstract from INAF open-access repository (openaccess.inaf.it/handle/20.500.12386/24805): 'We derive initial rotation, shape, and scattering properties ... from sparse and dense photometry based on the so-called Lommel-Seeliger ellipsoid'. It also cites the analytic brightness, 'fast rotation-period, pole-orientation, and shape analyses' and 'efficient Markov-chain Monte Carlo solutions'. The quoted conclusion is verbatim. 'Before more detailed modeling' is the claimant's reading of 'initial'. Crossref lists pages 227-241; INAF lists 227-237.

results.claim: Asteroids IV review: triaxial ellipsoid usually enough for noisy sparse data (cites Cellino 2009, Cellino & Dell'Oro 2012, Carbognani 2012); two shape params make period scan fast; pole accuracy from a few degrees to >20 deg.
results.source: Durech, Carry, Delbo, Kaasalainen, Viikinkoski 2015, Asteroids IV; arXiv:1502.04816
results.evidence: Text extracted from the arXiv PDF. 'When using noisy sparse data or only a limited number of data points, a simple shape model of a triaxial ellipsoid is usually sufficient...' cites 'Cellino et al., 2009; Cellino and Dell'Oro, 2012; Carbognani et al., 2012'. 'the shape is described by only two parameters (axes ratios) and the scanning of the period parameter space is much faster'. Pole accuracy: 'from a couple of degrees ... many dense lightcurves, to more than twenty degrees for models based on limited and noisy data.'

results.claim: Kaasalainen & Durech: sparse gives period and spin but crude shape; spin not affected by shape/albedo ambiguity; calibrated sparse needs phase curve fit, e.g. exponential-linear x LS+Lambert as in convexinv; prograde/retrograde ambiguity from insufficient data, not lambda+180.
results.source: Kaasalainen & Durech 2020, arXiv:2005.09947
results.evidence: Text extracted from the arXiv PDF. The quoted phrase ('successful inversion (though obviously crude for shape) ... very sparse photometry') is verbatim. 'The determination of the spin axis direction is also not affected by the shape/albedo ambiguity.' With calibrated sparse photometry 'it is necessary to fit also the phase curves', e.g. 'an exponential-linear phase function multiplied by a combination of Lomell-Seeliger and Lambert scattering (Kaasalainen et al., 2001)'. The paper cites Kaasalainen et al. 2001 and does not name convexinv. 'λ + 180° ambiguity has nothing to do with the prograde/retrograde ambiguity ... usually caused by insufficient data.'

results.claim: Kaasalainen & Durech recommend LM from many initial values; genetic algorithms poor (lose other minima); warn against inverse crime.
results.source: Kaasalainen & Durech 2020, arXiv:2005.09947
results.evidence: The quoted sentence on genetic algorithms is verbatim, followed by 'they typically lose the information on other eligible minima'. 'gradient-based optimisation procedures (in particular Levenberg-Marquardt ...) started from a variety of initial guesses are superior in both speed and accuracy.' Inverse crime: 'creating the data with the same model they are inverted with ... can result in much too overconfident solutions'. Again, 'as in convexinv' is the claimant's gloss.

results.claim: Hanus & Durech 2012: CSS (703) sparse-only, 0.1 mag precision (~12%), n=2-6; period stable but pole longitude often moved >=50 deg; accept only if rerun at n=3 (step 0.5 dP) gives similar unique solution; 7 of 13 CSS-only models agreed.
results.source: Hanus & Durech 2012, PSS 73, 75-79; arXiv:1301.7205
results.evidence: Text extracted from the arXiv PDF. AstDyS magnitudes are given 'to only one decimal place, so the accuracy is 0.1 mag at best'; CSS 'typical photometric accuracy was ∼12%'. Table 1 tests n=2-6 with Pstep 0.8 and 0.5 ΔP. Correct periods 'were always stable'. The quoted dispersion sentence (latitude ≲20°, longitude often ≳50°) is verbatim. Procedure: use n=6 and Pstep=0.5ΔP; if unique, 'rerun with n = 3 and Pstep = 0.5∆P. The model is then reliable if we get similar unique solutions.' 'in 7 cases out of 13, the solution was in a well agreement'.

results.claim: Hanus et al. 2011: AstDyS/MPC sparse from 689, 699, 703, E12, G96, 950, Hipparcos; weights USNO 0.3, Hip 0.3, CSS 0.15, La Palma 0.15, LONEOS 0.1, Siding Spring 0.1, Mt Lemmon 0.1; excluded high-scatter observatories; pole uncertainty +/-10-20 deg; 16 sparse-only models matched DAMIT.
results.source: Hanus, Durech, Broz et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134; arXiv:1104.4114
results.evidence: Text extracted from the arXiv PDF. Table 1 weights: 689 USNO 0.3, 699 LONEOS 0.1, 703 CSS 0.15, 950 La Palma 0.15, E12 Siding Spring 0.1, G96 Mt Lemmon 0.1, Hipparcos 0.3. Others (608, 644, 683, 691, 704, H07) get 0. Dense data have unity weight (~0.02 mag). The quoted ≳0.2 mag exclusion sentence is verbatim (691 is the example). 'We estimated the uncertainty in the pole direction as ±10–20°'. 'We obtained similar resulting models for all 16 asteroids.' The data source is named as AstDyS.

results.claim: Santana-Ros et al. 2017: DPAC chose ellipsoids because ~60-70 Gaia points cannot constrain a complex shape alone; sparse convex shapes usually low-resolution and angular.
results.source: Santana-Ros, Dudzinski, Bartczak 2017; arXiv:1705.05710
results.corrected_claim: The chapter says Gaia will observe each asteroid 50-70 times on average, not 60-70. It says this number of measurements 'is not enough to constrain a complex model shape by its own'. CPU cost is the second stated reason, which leads to an analytically computed LS triaxial ellipsoid. Convex models from sparse data are 'usually a low-resolution, "angular" convex shape'.
results.evidence: Text extracted from the arXiv PDF: 'on average Gaia will observe each asteroid 50-70 times during 5 years. Despite of the high data quality, this number of measurements is not enough to constrain a complex model shape by its own. Moreover, processing such enormous amount of data would be highly CPU demanding.' And: 'the shape model is usually a low-resolution, "angular" convex shape'.

results.claim: Nortunen et al.: ellipsoid brightness-variation model tested on DAMIT-based synthetic populations; robust only for population distributions of elongation and spin latitude, not individuals; local irregularities shift elongation even without noise.
results.source: Nortunen, Kaasalainen, Durech, Cibulkova, Ali-Lagoa, Hanus 2017, A&A 601, A139; arXiv:1703.07178
results.evidence: Text extracted from the arXiv PDF. The model is a population-scale observable using shape elongation p and spin latitude beta; it is 'a coarse shape approximation for individual targets'. The forward model uses 'asteroid models from DAMIT' with transformations. 'The p-shift is inevitable: even in the absence of noise, near-spherical targets ... because of local shape irregularities.' The quoted sentence on tolerating the crude shape model is verbatim.

results.claim: (103) Hera: convex poles (83.0, 39.0) and (269.7, 56.8); LS ellipsoid (74.1, 39.0) and (263.1, 51.0); same period to ~1e-4 h; differences ~7 deg.
results.source: Wang, Wang, Muinonen, Han 2019, PSS 167, 17-22; DOI 10.1016/j.pss.2019.01.007
results.evidence: Abstract via the Semantic Scholar API (ScienceDirect and ResearchGate returned 403). Convex: '(83.0°, 39.0°) and (269.7°, 56.8°)', periods 23.74264 h and 23.74267 h. LS ellipsoid on 'the same data': '(74.1°, 39.0°) and (263.1°, 51.0°)', 23.74262 h and 23.74263 h. Period differences are ≤5e-5 h. My calculated pole differences are 6.9° and 6.4°. Caveat: the abstract says only 'existing and new photometric data' from Chinese and SARA telescopes. 'Mostly dense' could not be checked without the full text. PSS 167, 17-22 (March 2019) confirmed via Crossref.

results.claim: Durech & Hanus EPSC-DPS2025-96: Prague pipeline on Catalina, Mt Lemmon, Pan-STARRS, ZTF, ATLAS, TESS, ASAS-SN, USNO, Gaia DR3; ~23,000 models from ~330,000 asteroids.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2025, EPSC-DPS2025-96 (conference abstract)
results.evidence: Copernicus abstract titled 'Asteroid phase curves reconstructed with light curve inversion – prospects for LSST'. It lists Catalina, Mt. Lemmon, Pan-STARRS, ZTF, ATLAS, TESS, ASAS-SN, USNO and Gaia DR3. 'From about 330,000 processed asteroids, we were able to derive unique spin solutions and corresponding convex shape models for about 23,000.' Caveat on the quote: 'hundreds of data points per asteroid' refers only to ATLAS ('ATLAS photometry in cyan and orange filters with hundreds of data points per asteroid'), not to the combined data. That is far more points per object than typical MPC sparse sets.

results.claim: DAMIT software v0.2.1 is Durech's C translation of Kaasalainen's Fortran; convexinv optimizes all parameters with SH shape; conjgradinv polishes only facet areas; lightcurve files flag relative (0)/calibrated (1); scattering is Lambert + Lommel-Seeliger.
results.source: DAMIT software download and documentation pages
results.corrected_claim: The software page confirms v0.2.1, written by Kaasalainen in Fortran and converted to C by Durech. It describes convexinv as optimizing all parameters with spherical harmonics (quote verbatim) and conjgradinv as optimizing only the shape, using facet areas directly, for the final stage. The download page does not state the scattering law or the lightcurve format. Both appear on the DAMIT documentation page. That page describes the database's lc.txt export: each lightcurve header gives the point count and a 0/1 code for relative (0) or calibrated (1). Its models table has a light-scattering column with two options, 'LSL = Lambert + Lommel-Seeliger' or 'H = Hapke'. So LSL is one of two laws used for DAMIT models. The pages read do not say it is convexinv's only law, though that may be in the manuals inside the download, which I did not open.
results.evidence: damit.cuni.cz software_download: version v0.2.1; Fortran by Kaasalainen, converted to C by Durech. convexinv 'optimizes all parameters and uses spherical harmonics functions for shape representation'; conjgradinv optimizes only shape with facet areas. The page itself has no scattering or format details. Documentation page: 'header line that gives the number of points followed by 0/1 code for a relative (0) or calibrated (1) light curve'. Models table column 'Used light-scattering model (LSM): LSL = Lambert + Lommel-Seeliger; H = Hapke'.

findings.claim: DAMIT/Asteroids@home uniqueness criterion: a period (or pole) is unique if every other local minimum has chi2 above chi2_tr = (1 + 0.5*sqrt(2/nu)) * chi2_min, with nu = N_points - N_params. This replaced the earlier fixed 5% rule. The authors call it empirical: the 1/2 factor was tuned so the threshold is not too strict, and the old 5% level corresponds to nu = 200.
findings.source: Durech, Hanus & Ali-Lagoa 2018, A&A 617, A57, arXiv:1807.02083
findings.quote: χ2tr = (1 + 0.5 √2/ν) χ2min. This is nothing more than an empirical prescription to take into account the number of measurements

findings.claim: How the parameters are counted for nu: 3 spin parameters (lambda, beta, P) + 3 phase-function parameters + (n+1)^2 shape coefficients for a convex model with spherical-harmonic degree/order n, or 2 axis ratios for an ellipsoid. In this pipeline the ellipsoid is a scan in its own right: periodograms are computed with convex n=3, convex n=6 and ellipsoids. The unique periods from n=3 and n=6 must agree.
findings.source: Durech, Hanus & Ali-Lagoa 2018, A&A 617, A57, arXiv:1807.02083
findings.quote: three parameters for the spin state, three parameters to fit the photometric phase function, and (n + 1)2 shape parameters

findings.claim: For Gaia DR2 the factor was raised to k=1: chi2_tr = (1 + sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min. Parameter counts: p=6 for ellipsoids (P, lambda, beta, linear phase slope, a/c, b/c) and p=20 for convex n=3 (16 shape coefficients). Periodograms with all RMS < 0.005 mag were rejected as noise-fitting. Only one period could have RMS < 0.01.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91, arXiv:1810.04485
findings.quote: This is an arbitrary borderline that is based on a trade-off between the total number of new models and their contamination with incorrect models.

findings.claim: Lowell (MPC-recalibrated) + Gaia DR2: k in chi2_tr = (1 + k sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min was calibrated against LCDB U>=3 periods (correct = within 10%). Convex models with w=0.01: k=1 gave 287 models (87% correct), k=1/2 gave 522 (86%), k=1/3 gave 641 (83%). Ellipsoids with k=1 gave 710 models (90%). Lowell data got weight w=0.01 relative to Gaia (0.1 vs 0.01 mag). The adopted value is printed as k=3 for convex (possibly 1/3, since the table only tests 1, 1/2, 1/3) and k=1 for ellipsoids. About 15% of accepted periods were still wrong before the further checks.
findings.source: Durech, Hanus & Vanco 2019, A&A 631, A2, arXiv:1909.09395
findings.quote: reliable errors of individual measurements are not known and are often dominated by errors other than Gaussian random noise.

findings.claim: Gaia DR3: chi2_tr = (1 + sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min, the RMS of every local minimum had to exceed 0.01, and the minimum relative error was set to 0.01. Convex degree 3 was used with 15 optimized shape coefficients (size fixed), plus the inertia check (<1.1) and the mirror-pole check. Against LCDB U=3 periods the false-solution rate was 5/848.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24, arXiv:2305.10798
findings.quote: With 848 periods in total, this represents a false solution rate of just ∼0.6%.

findings.claim: ASAS-SN: the threshold factor p was chosen per model family from the false-solution rate against LCDB flag-3 periods. Below p=0.5 the false rate rises quickly. They adopted p=0.5 for convex inversion and p=0.6 for triaxial ellipsoids, giving about 3% of convex periods inconsistent with LCDB.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2021, A&A 654, A48, arXiv:2107.10027
findings.quote: So we select p = 0.5 as an optimal value in the CI and p = 0.6 in the tri-axial ellipsoid shape analyses.

findings.claim: Older criterion used for AstDyS/MPC sparse data. The best period must have at least 10% lower chi2 than all others, and only one pole (up to lambda+-180) may be at least 10% lower. For half/double periods, the model was rejected if the chi2 at 2P or P/2 was below 1.1 chi2(P).
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134, arXiv:1104.4114
findings.quote: the best period has at least 10% lower χ2 than all other periods in the scanned interval

findings.claim: The DAMIT team says formal significance tests on chi2 cannot be used for survey sparse data because of systematic errors, so they rely on empirical tests calibrated against DAMIT. Test 1 is a 5% chi2 margin outside Pmin +- 0.5 Pmin^2/dT, chosen to keep false positives near 1%. Other tests: n=3 and n=6 periods must agree; Pmin < 20 h without a prior; at most two poles more than 30 deg apart; inertia; bootstrap; visual check.
findings.source: Durech, Hanus, Oszkiewicz & Vanco 2016, A&A 587, A48, arXiv:1601.02909
findings.quote: We could not use formal statistical tools to decide whether the lowest χ2 value is statistically significant or not

findings.claim: Bootstrap test, Lowell sparse data: each surviving model's data were resampled (same number of points, randomly selected) and the full period search was rerun with convex shapes or ellipsoids. The model was kept only if the bootstrap best-fit period matched the original.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2016, A&A 587, A48, arXiv:1601.02909
findings.quote: the model was considered stable only if the best-fit period Pmin from the bootstrapped data agreed with that from the original data.

findings.claim: Physical and mirror-pole filters used with every convexinv result. Inertia ratio must be <1.1. With two poles, |beta1-beta2| < 50 deg and mod(|lambda1-lambda2|, 180) > 120 deg, matching the lambda+-180 ambiguity for near-ecliptic geometry. Models that formally fit but are unrealistically elongated or flat were rejected visually.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2016, A&A 587, A48, arXiv:1601.02909
findings.quote: The ratio of the moment of inertia along the principal axis to that along the actual rotation axis should be less than 1.1.

findings.claim: ATLAS: uncertainties came from 100 bootstrap resamples per model. Resampling was with replacement and kept the number of points in each filter (c, o). Convexinv was restarted from the original spin, and the standard deviations of lambda, beta, P and c-o give the errors.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2020, A&A 643, A59, arXiv:2010.01820
findings.quote: We created one hundred bootstrapped data samples for every full and partial model.

findings.claim: Bootstrap convex inversion used as a period-reliability score: 25 resamples per asteroid, filters resampled independently. N_BS counts resamples whose best period matches the original within 1%. Per the publisher page, asteroids with N_BS=25 had about 99.5% probability of a correct period; 885 of 904 periods agreed with LCDB within 5%.
findings.source: Durech, Vavra, Vanco & Erasmus 2022, Front. Astron. Space Sci. 9, 809771, DOI:10.3389/fspas.2022.809771
findings.quote: If the best period is always the same for all BS samples, it is likely to be the actual rotation period.

findings.claim: Jackknife period-stability test: split the data into 10 random parts, drop one (10%), redo the period search, repeat 10 times. Keep only asteroids where at least 9 of 10 jackknife periods match the original within 0.1%. Separately, 20 asteroids whose convex and ellipsoid periods disagreed were excluded.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24, arXiv:2305.10798
findings.quote: selected only asteroids for which all ten jackknife periods were the same (within 0.1%) as the original period

findings.claim: Removing 10% of points (2-5 points for Gaia DR2) usually left the period unchanged. In 44 cases the period stayed the same but fell below the chi2_tr threshold, and in 1 case it changed, i.e. many sparse solutions sit at the edge of uniqueness.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91, arXiv:1810.04485
findings.quote: with our definition of χ2tr, we are at the critical limit of the number of data points in many cases.

findings.claim: Sparse-only (AstDyS/MPC) models were tested in two ways. (a) Rerun with randomly reduced data (90%): 5 of 63 lost uniqueness, none switched to a different solution. (b) Ten 'mock' shapes per model, with synthetic photometry at the real epochs and noise, were inverted: most were recovered, pole scatter about +-10 deg.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134, arXiv:1104.4114
findings.quote: The typical uncertainty in pole direction was ±10◦ and, for the period, ∼0.1 times the difference between the two local minimums

findings.claim: Synthetic test with 50 random poles per model (synthetic data at the real epochs plus real relative residuals): pole errors were sigma ~10 deg in beta and ~5 deg/cos(beta) in lambda. Inversion succeeds about 30% less often for |beta| ~ 0 than for |beta| > 53 deg, which biases sparse-data samples toward high-latitude poles.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134, arXiv:1104.4114
findings.quote: typical uncertainty that we can expect in pole determination by the lightcurve inversion method, which is ∼5◦/ cos β in λ and ∼10◦ in β

findings.claim: Catalina-only (MPC 703) sparse data: correct models were recovered at most shape resolutions n=2-6, while wrong unique solutions appeared mainly at n=6 (sometimes n=4-5) and never at n=2-3. Recommendation: scan with n=6 and Pstep=0.5*dP, then rerun with n=3. Accept only if both give similar unique solutions.
findings.source: Hanus & Durech 2012, Planet. Space Sci. 73, 75, arXiv:1301.7205
findings.quote: we got unique solutions for different resolutions n and period steps Pstep only rarely and never for n = 2 or n = 3

findings.claim: Catalina-only (703) data, at least 50 points, 185 asteroids with independent DAMIT models: 13 unique solutions, of which only 7 agreed with the independent model. The authors list three causes: low amplitude relative to noise, too few data for the number of parameters, and survey systematics. A suspiciously low ('too perfect') RMS can flag a random solution, but not reliably.
findings.source: Hanus & Durech 2012, Planet. Space Sci. 73, 75, arXiv:1301.7205
findings.quote: Only in 7 cases the solution was in an agreement with the model based on a different data set

findings.claim: Systematics in MPC astrometric-survey magnitudes (citing Oszkiewicz et al. 2011): errors depend on apparent magnitude, with saturation for bright objects and poor background subtraction for faint ones. Most incorrect CSS-only models were for brighter asteroids. Typical CSS accuracy is about 12%; the data are useful mainly for amplitudes >= 0.3 mag.
findings.source: Hanus & Durech 2012, Planet. Space Sci. 73, 75, arXiv:1301.7205
findings.quote: For the brightest asteroids, the images are saturated, and for the faintest, the background subtraction is imperfect.

findings.claim: Per-observatory screening of AstDyS (MPC) sparse photometry. Magnitudes are mostly given to 0.1 mag. A phase function a*exp(-alpha/b)+c*alpha+d was fit per sparse lightcurve and residual statistics were tabulated (Table 1: median residual, weight relative to dense data at ~0.02 mag): 704 LINEAR 0.42 (rejected), 691 Spacewatch 0.24 (rejected), 703 CSS 0.19 (w=0.15), 699 LONEOS 0.18 (w=0.1), G96 Mt Lemmon 0.17 (w=0.1), E12 0.15 (w=0.1), 950 0.15 (w=0.15), 689 USNO 0.15 (w=0.3), Hipparcos 0.11 (w=0.3).
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134, arXiv:1104.4114
findings.quote: Observatories with a high median or “FWHM” value (≳0.2 mag for both) are not suitable for the lightcurve inversion

findings.claim: Review chapter: for noisy sparse data or few points, a triaxial ellipsoid (2 shape parameters) is usually enough to get the correct period and pole, and it scans much faster. Survey data are rarely better than 0.1 mag, so many physically acceptable models fit to the noise level.
findings.source: Durech, Carry, Delbo, Kaasalainen & Viikinkoski 2015, in Asteroids IV (Univ. Arizona Press), arXiv:1502.04816
findings.quote: a simple shape model of a triaxial ellipsoid is usually sufficient to model the data and to derive the correct period and spin vector orientation

findings.claim: The resolution limit of photometry: once a model fits to the noise level, extra shape freedom (nonconvex detail) does not improve the fit. The authors recommend producing several solutions with different model types and parameters, and caution about the results.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2015, Asteroids IV, arXiv:1502.04816
findings.quote: Nonconvex models seldom fit lightcurves better than convex ones simply because the latter typically already fit the data down to noise level.

findings.claim: Why the DAMIT pipeline scans periods with ellipsoids: geometric-scattering ellipsoid brightness is analytic (about 100x faster), and with a > b > c the rotation is automatically about the maximum-inertia axis. A flexible convex model can fit sparse data at a wrong period with a nonphysical shape. In practice the best period from the ellipsoid scan is then refined with convex shapes for the pole.
findings.source: Durech, Hanus & Ali-Lagoa 2018, A&A 617, A57, arXiv:1807.02083
findings.quote: convex models can formally fit the data with an incorrect period with a nonphysical shape due to their flexibility

findings.claim: Ellipsoids (Kaasalainen & Durech 2007 geometric model) often give a unique, correct period when convex models give many equally good periods. Results are labelled C, E or CE (both found the same unique period). Caveat: for (540) Rosamunde the ellipsoid's best period (7.82 h) passed all tests but was wrong; the DAMIT period 9.35 h was only the convex runner-up.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2016, A&A 587, A48, arXiv:1601.02909
findings.quote: The accuracy of this simplified model is sufficient to reveal the correct rotation period as a significant minimum of χ2 in the period parameter space.

findings.claim: Against LCDB, convex models produce false half-period solutions (one maximum per rotation), which ellipsoids avoid. Both families are unreliable for N < ~30 (success rate rises above 0.5 only for N > 30), and convex fits tend toward wrong shorter periods.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91, arXiv:1810.04485
findings.quote: Ellipsoidal models do not have this disadvantage of producing false half periods, but the periods based on a small number of points are often wrong.

findings.claim: Main limitation of the ellipsoid: it fails for non-double-sinusoid lightcurves. In DR3 the ellipsoid periodograms gave 16,010 unique periods; after convex modelling and filters, 5,784 ellipsoid-based and 6,269 convex-based models survived jackknife. 3,431 had both, and 20 where the two periods disagreed were discarded.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24, arXiv:2305.10798
findings.quote: ellipsoidal shape models are insufficient when an asteroid’s light curve significantly differs from a simple double sinusoidal curve.

findings.claim: Convex inversion often fits P and P/2 about equally well, while ellipsoids usually prefer the true P. Convex P/2 solutions tend to be nonphysical (rotation about the longest axis). The ellipsoid is used only for the period; the shape comes from convex inversion.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2021, A&A 654, A48, arXiv:2107.10027
findings.quote: light curve inversion with tri-axial ellipsoids usually favors only the correct period P

findings.claim: MCMC inversion of Gaia DR3 with both triaxial ellipsoids and convex shapes: for most objects the ellipsoid poles match the convex poles. 15% of convex shapes were rejected. (Read from the abstract only; the full text returned 403.)
findings.quote: The assumption of ellipsoid shape for sparse datasets is sufficient for estimating the spin pole longitude and latitude.

findings.claim: Simulated Gaia sparse photometry of complex (DAMIT) shapes, inverted with ellipsoids: the recovered ellipsoids are close to the best-fitting ellipsoids of the true shapes, and the volume error is about 10%.
findings.source: Carbognani et al. 2012, Planet. Space Sci. 73, 80, arXiv:1903.12633, DOI:10.1016/j.pss.2011.12.002
findings.quote: the error on the asteroid volume (relative to a complex shape) is generally low, usually around 10%.

findings.claim: Low-resolution convex shapes from sparse data are not real shapes. With n=3 they show sharp edges and triangular pole-on outlines, while period and pole are much less sensitive to the resolution. Durech et al. 2016 likewise found sparse-data shapes more angular than dense-lightcurve shapes, often with artificial sharp edges.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91, arXiv:1810.04485
findings.quote: convex shape models derived from DR2 data should not be taken as real shapes

findings.claim: Lowell (recalibrated MPC) models vs 279 DAMIT models: 275 had the same period and pole difference < 50 deg, with mean 15 deg and median 13 deg, taken as the typical pole error (DAMIT poles ~5-10 deg). Four were clearly different. The false-positive rate is about a few percent, but DAMIT is biased against low-amplitude, long-period objects, so the real rate may be higher.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2016, A&A 587, A48, arXiv:1601.02909
findings.quote: the mean value is 15◦ and the median 13◦, which can be interpreted as a typical error in the pole determination

findings.claim: Lowell+WISE vs 246 DAMIT models: 5 periods differed by only ~1e-4 relative (adjacent local minima) yet gave very different poles, and 4 were completely different. In the 237 matching cases the mean pole difference was 12 deg and the median 9 deg. Axis ratios (a/b)_DAMIT/(a/b)_sparse = 1.06 +- 0.13 and b/c 1.06 +- 0.18, so sparse models come out slightly less elongated.
findings.source: Durech, Hanus & Ali-Lagoa 2018, A&A 617, A57, arXiv:1807.02083
findings.quote: the difference between the poles was mainly less than 30◦, with only a few cases having a pole difference up to 60◦

findings.claim: Gaia DR2 models vs 44 DAMIT models: mean pole difference 20 deg, with 7 outliers > 60 deg. One DAMIT sparse-only model was wrong (wrong local minimum), 5 were adjacent local minima, and 1 had a completely different period.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91, arXiv:1810.04485
findings.quote: their periods were the same within the errorbars and the mean difference between their pole directions was 20◦.

findings.claim: Caution about using DAMIT as ground truth: in 33 cases DR3 periods differed from DAMIT, and most of those DAMIT models were judged wrong. They were typically sparse-only, often Lowell (MPC) based. Only 2 of the 33 DR3 solutions were clearly wrong.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24, arXiv:2305.10798
findings.quote: These incorrect DAMIT solutions are usually based on sparse data only, often on the Lowell Observatory dataset with poor photometric quality.

findings.claim: ASAS-SN sparse models vs DAMIT: pole differences rarely exceed 30 deg. Four solutions were inconsistent, including two with twice the DAMIT period.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2021, A&A 654, A48, arXiv:2107.10027
findings.quote: The difference is rarely larger than 30◦, which suggests a good consistency between our solutions and previous estimates.

findings.claim: Expected pole uncertainty by data type: below 5 deg for rich multi-apparition dense data; 5-10 deg (beta) for dense plus sparse; 10-30 deg in beta and 10-30 deg/cos(beta) in lambda for few-apparition dense plus sparse, or sparse only. Sparse data were weighted 0.3 (689 USNO) and 0.15 (703 CSS), and Lowell data 0.1, relative to dense data.
findings.quote: ∼10−30◦ in β and ∼10−30◦/cos β in λ for models based on combined few-apparition dense data with sparse-in-time measurements or only sparse-in-time data

findings.claim: Catalina-only (703) models: about 1e-4 to 1e-5 h period uncertainty and 20-40 deg pole uncertainty. Sparse-only shapes are angular, with sharp edges and planar areas; adding about 10 or more dense lightcurves from 2 or more apparitions smooths them and improves the fit to occultation chords.
findings.source: Hanus et al. 2013, A&A 551, A67, arXiv:1301.6943
findings.quote: the typical uncertainty of the sidereal rotational period is ∼10−4 −10−5 h and of the pole direction 20–40◦

findings.claim: Occultation validation: scaling convex models to multi-chord occultations often rejects one of the two mirror poles, and sizes come out to about 10%.
findings.quote: In many cases, occultations allow us to reject one of two possible pole solutions that were derived from photometry.

findings.claim: A close analogue of our ellipsoid aspect model, applied to ZTF alert photometry (sHG1G2: phase function plus a spin/oblateness aspect term). Spins of 6,499 objects compared with the literature (mostly DAMIT): the angular separation peaks near 20 deg and half agree within 35 deg. About 60% agree within 1 sigma and 95% within 3 sigma, suggesting realistic uncertainties.
findings.quote: The distribution peaks around 20◦, with half of the SSOs agreeing below 35◦.

findings.claim: Model-complexity argument for an aspect model on sparse survey data. The richer sHG1G2 is often not needed: for near-spherical bodies, obliquity near 0 or 180 deg, or a narrow aspect-angle range, it fits no better than HG1G2. The authors recommend fitting all models 'from the most robust to the most informative' and falling back to the simpler one in those cases.
findings.source: Carry et al. 2024, A&A 687, A38, arXiv:2403.20179
findings.quote: the predictions by HG or HG1G2 fit equally well the data as sHG1G2, although the latter has more degrees of freedom.

findings.claim: The same model class as ours: geometric-scattering triaxial ellipsoids fit to per-apparition mean brightness and brightness dispersion in Lowell (MPC) data. A synthetic test with DAMIT shapes and Hapke scattering showed lambda is reliable statistically but beta is biased. A 'model noise' term (0.06 mag) was needed for the non-ellipsoid mismatch. Noise is larger for fainter asteroids (0.08 mag was best for bright DAMIT objects).
findings.source: Cibulkova, Durech, Vokrouhlicky, Kaasalainen & Oszkiewicz 2016, A&A 596, A57, arXiv:1610.02790, DOI:10.1051/0004-6361/201629192
findings.quote: determination of λ is reliable in a statistical sense, while (ii) determination of β is subject to systematic bias

findings.claim: Spin-axis longitudes for more than 350,000 asteroids from mean-brightness variation with ecliptic longitude (sin 2*lambda fit) in the Lowell/MPC database. Reliable only for peak-to-peak variation > 0.15 mag and at least ~50 observations. Adding a first harmonic overfits the noisy data for 1.7% of objects. The MPC data mix many sources with different, sometimes time-variable, systematic and random errors.
findings.source: Bowell et al. 2014, Meteorit. Planet. Sci. 49, 95, arXiv:1310.3617, DOI:10.1111/maps.12230
findings.quote: low precision (generally rounded to 0.1 mag) and low accuracy (rms magnitude uncertainties of 0.2 to 0.3 mag are typical)

findings.claim: Problems with MPC photometry: non-standard filters or no calibration; no colour transformation to V; no per-observation uncertainties (they must be back-calculated per observatory); storage at 0.1 mag precision; default G; rotation amplitude ignored. MPC applies observatory-dependent corrections to address the ~0.4 mag systematic error reported by Juric et al.
findings.quote: Reporting observations to the Minor Planet Center (MPC) in non-standard filters and/or without accurate calibration.

findings.claim: Catalog H values (MPCORB/AstDyS/JPL) for H > 10-12 are systematically too bright, by 0.4-0.5 mag near H = 14; the suspected cause is the magnitudes reported by surveys. Mechanisms: clear/no-filter data reported without a filter code are treated as B and converted to V; R-calibrated data reported as V are off by 0.4-0.5 mag; single default G=0.15 and V-R=0.40 values introduce taxonomy-dependent offsets.
findings.source: Pravec et al. 2012, Icarus 221, 365 (no arXiv; author PDF)
findings.quote: if observations taken with a clear or no filter are reported without a filter code, the magnitude estimates are taken as B band observations

findings.claim: Station- and catalog-dependent biases in MPC photometry, analysed on about 500,000 MPC observations. For 703 and G96 the bias dropped by more than 0.3 and 0.1 mag in summer 2018, when the reference catalog switched from Gaia DR1 to DR2. G96 bias rises again after summer 2022 and is not corrected. Most V-band reporters, including 703/G96 with UCAC catalogs, show about +0.25 mag bias.
findings.source: Hoffmann et al. 2024 (DePhOCUS), Icarus, arXiv:2408.07474, DOI:10.1016/j.icarus.2024.116366
findings.quote: This drop perfectly corresponds to the switch from Gaia DR1 to DR2 as reference star catalog

findings.claim: 704 (LINEAR, USNO-A catalogs): bias is about 0 mag in the upper galactic hemisphere and about -0.5 mag in the lower, attributed to separate north/south catalog calibrations. Its bias also grows with apparent magnitude and was not constant before 2006. Sky-position-dependent offsets like this can masquerade as aspect-dependent brightness changes.
findings.source: Hoffmann et al. 2024 (DePhOCUS), Icarus, arXiv:2408.07474
findings.quote: the upper hemisphere has a bias around 0 mag, while the lower hemisphere has a bias around −0.5 mag.

findings.claim: Other station behaviour among the seven largest stations (C57, 703, T08, T05, 704, G96, F51). T05/T08 (ATLAS) are stable in time, but observations fainter than ~19 mag are biased bright (selection near the detection limit). F51 reports fast movers too faint (trailing). C57 (TESS) shows no systematic photometric deviation despite large astrometric errors. With 0.10 mag precision and no lightcurve correction, a residual RMS of about 0.25 mag is the expected floor.
findings.source: Hoffmann et al. 2024 (DePhOCUS), Icarus, arXiv:2408.07474
findings.quote: for apparent magnitudes larger than 19 there is an increase of bias, meaning that low SNR observations have a higher bias

findings.claim: Processing recipe for multi-survey sparse data from MPC/AstDyS (CSS, USNO, ZTF from AstDyS; ATLAS, ASAS-SN, Gaia, TESS): treat each survey+filter as a separate internally calibrated dataset normalized to unity, sigma-clip, weight by expected RMS, and use one shared phase function (a stated approximation). Uniqueness via chi2_tr with k=0.5 and dP/P = P/(2T); a period uncertainty of about dP/20 is used.
findings.quote: All individual measurements within each sparse dataset (i.e. specific survey and photometric filter) are internally calibrated; therefore, we process each dataset separately.

findings.claim: Recent case of convexinv run on MPC-retrieved sparse photometry: (16583) Oersted, about 20 km, using CSS, ATLAS c/o, ASAS-SN, Gaia DR3, ZTF g/r and Pan-STARRS from MPC and AstDyS. A well-defined global period minimum below the chi2 threshold gave a single pole, and the model was checked against a multi-chord occultation.
findings.source: Hanus, Delbo, Pokorny, Marchis & Esposito 2025, A&A (accepted), arXiv:2510.05843
findings.quote: The photometric points were retrieved from the Minor Planet Center and the AstDyS databases, and span multiple apparition epochs

findings.claim: ATLAS-specific handling. About 15% of points were removed as outliers beyond 2.5 RMS from a phase-curve fit. The c-o colour is a free scale factor (magnitude offset) between filters. Separate phase slopes for c and o improve fits only marginally. The one-day cadence causes aliasing near 12/24/48 h. Both full convex and ellipsoid scans were run (C/E/CE tags), and only about 5,000 of about 100,000 asteroids got a reliable period.
findings.source: Durech et al. 2020, A&A 643, A59, arXiv:2010.01820
findings.quote: splitting photometry into two colors and fitting them with different slopes improves the fit, but usually not very significantly.

findings.claim: Limit for low amplitudes in ATLAS data, about 10 years of forced photometry: for (10253) Westerwald (folded amplitude 0.12 mag) convexinv found no unique solution until points with errors > 0.2 mag were removed. Even then the pole was unconstrained beyond 'retrograde'. Spin errors came from 1,000 bootstraps resampling c and o separately.
findings.source: Erasmus, Durech et al. 2026, preprint, arXiv:2609.07404
findings.quote: there are many models with this rotation period but with different spin-axis orientations that fit the data to the same level of residuals

findings.claim: Low-amplitude and long-period bias in sparse-data modelling. Survey photometry at 0.1-0.2 mag misses most low-amplitude asteroids. Dense follow-up of (830) Petropolitana gave P = 169.52 h, versus the 37.347 h sparse-only DAMIT model of Hanus et al. 2016 (found by scanning only up to 100 h).
findings.source: Marciniak et al. 2018, A&A 610, A7, arXiv:1711.01893
findings.quote: very low photometric accuracy (0.1 - 0.2 mag on average, Hanuš et al. 2011), so the modelling is missing most of the low-amplitude population

findings.claim: Simulations of 10,000 Gaia-like sparse datasets with noise, inverted with an ellipsoid genetic algorithm: failures and biases concentrate in quasi-spherical bodies and low pole latitudes, where the amplitude is comparable to the noise. Adding one dense lightcurve reduces wrong solutions when N < 50.
findings.source: Santana-Ros et al. 2015, MNRAS, arXiv:1504.02809
findings.quote: the results are biased for asteroids having quasi-spherical shapes and low pole latitudes.

findings.claim: Bayesian alternative to fixed chi2 thresholds: an MCMC posterior over convex shapes and spins, with random and systematic errors modelled and observations weighted through priors. A separate uncertainty model is used for triaxial-ellipsoid inversion; validated on (21) Lutetia against the Rosetta-based model. The abstract does not mention AIC/BIC.
findings.source: Muinonen, Torppa, Wang, Cellino & Penttila 2020, A&A 642, A138, DOI:10.1051/0004-6361/202038036
findings.quote: We consider both random and systematic uncertainties (errors) in the observations, and assign weights to the observations with the help of Bayesian a priori probability densities.

findings.claim: Closest thing to cross-validation in the sparse-survey literature: a period-quality classifier trained and cross-validated on 805 asteroids with known periods. Contamination of 'reliable' periods was estimated at 4% from asteroids fitted independently in more than one opposition. No paper we read checks a model by predicting withheld lightcurves.
findings.quote: Subsequent consideration of asteroids with multiple lightcurve fits indicate a 4% contamination in these ‘reliable’ periods.

findings.claim: Test for whether shape detail is real: fit with two different shape parameterizations (octantoids and subdivision surfaces). Only features both reproduce are taken as supported by the data. Shape uncertainty is estimated by jackknife (leave one image out).
findings.source: Viikinkoski, Hanus, Kaasalainen, Marchis & Durech 2017, A&A, arXiv:1708.05191
findings.quote: The usage of different shape representations allows us to separate the effects of parametrization from the actual features supported by the data.

findings.claim: Data volume needed: Gaia's ~0.01 mag photometry needs tens of points, while ground-based sparse data need hundreds. Shapes from few points are sensitive to the number of points and the resolution; only the a/b of the dynamically equivalent ellipsoid is treated as a stable shape parameter.
findings.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24, arXiv:2305.10798
findings.quote: With Gaia, we need tens of data points, while with less accurate photometry we would need hundreds of them

findings.claim: The DAMIT software page offers version 0.2.1 (C translation by J. Durech of M. Kaasalainen's Fortran code), with brief manuals and example lightcurves. convexinv optimizes all parameters with a spherical-harmonics shape; conjgradinv optimizes facet areas only, for final 'polishing'; lcgenerator computes synthetic lightcurves. period_scan was not named in the page summary we read.
findings.source: DAMIT software download page (Astronomical Institute, Charles University), accessed 2026-10-05
findings.quote: optimizes all parameters and uses spherical harmonics functions for shape representation

research.notes:
How this was done: arXiv PDFs were downloaded to the scratchpad (C:\Users\kn18001\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\C--Users-kn18001-Documents\98a1f892-0efb-441d-a311-b800785b2496\scratchpad\papers\*.txt, converted with pymupdf) and read directly. Quotes are verbatim from those texts (ligatures normalized).

Exceptions to direct reading:
- Durech et al. 2022 (Frontiers) quotes came through WebFetch of the publisher page.
- MacLennan et al. 2026 and Muinonen et al. 2020: abstracts only, via the Semantic Scholar API. aanda.org returned 403 or a JS check, which I did not try to bypass. No NASA ADS pages were used.

Gaps and caveats:
1. Durech et al. 2009 (A&A 493, 291, USNO sparse data) has no arXiv version and the publisher page was blocked. I only know it through Hanus 2011: USNO-Flagstaff sparse data, typical error 8-10%.
2. A search-engine snippet (not the paper) suggests MacLennan 2026 used AIC = 2N ln(rms) + 2N_P to compare ellipsoid and convex fits, with l_max = 4 (28 parameters). Unverified.
3. I found no paper that validates a model by predicting withheld lightcurves. The literature instead uses bootstrap (Durech 2016/2020/2022, Erasmus 2026), jackknife with 10% removal (Durech & Hanus 2018/2023), reduction to 90% (Hanus 2011), a mock-object or synthetic-pole injection test (Hanus 2011, Cibulkova 2016), stability across shape resolutions (Hanus & Durech 2012), and comparison with DAMIT, LCDB and occultations.
4. I found no BIC/AIC use for choosing convexinv resolution. Durech 2016 explicitly says formal chi2 significance cannot be used because of systematics. All the chi2_tr factors (k = 0.5, 1; fixed 5% or 10%) are empirical and tuned against LCDB/DAMIT false-positive rates.
5. Important: these thresholds decide period/pole uniqueness within one model family. They are not a test of whether convex beats ellipsoid. In the DAMIT pipeline the ellipsoid is the period finder, convex is used for pole and shape, and agreement between the two (CE) is a reliability flag; disagreements were discarded in DR3.

My inferences (not from the sources), suggested for the comparison:
(a) Compare both models on the same raw points with the same weights. Use nu = N - p, with p_ell ≈ 3 spin + phase parameters + 2 axes, and p_conv ≈ 3 + phase + 15-16 for n=3.
(b) Call the convex model a real improvement only if chi2_conv < chi2_ell / (1 + k*sqrt(2/nu)) with k = 0.5-1. For nu ≈ 500 that means roughly a 3-6% chi2 drop; an AIC-like penalty of 2*Delta_p ≈ 26-28 units with chi2/nu ≈ 1 is similar.
(c) Also require: the same period and pole from both models, or C=E; a stable result under 10x10% jackknife and bootstrap; n=3 vs n=6 agreement; inertia ratio < 1.1; RMS not below the noise floor ('too perfect'); and, where DAMIT dense or occultation models exist, a pole within about 20-30 deg (published means 9-20 deg, outliers > 50-60 deg usually mean an adjacent local minimum).
(d) MPC-specific risks for our mean-brightness and amplitude aspect fit:
   - 0.1 mag quantization adds about 0.029 mag rms (0.1/sqrt(12)), and for 0.1-0.2 mag amplitudes the effect on per-apparition amplitude estimates is not negligible.
   - Per-station zero-point steps (703 and G96 in 2018 at the Gaia DR2 switch; G96 after 2022) and sky-position-dependent offsets (704: about 0.5 mag between galactic hemispheres) shift per-apparition mean levels and can mimic an aspect signal. Split datasets by station, filter and reference-catalog epoch, each with its own offset, as in Athanasopoulos 2022 and Durech 2020 (c-o offset).
   - ATLAS T05/T08 measurements fainter than about 19 mag are biased bright.
   - Survey-only sparse models in DAMIT (Lowell- or CSS-based) are not reliable ground truth (Durech & Hanus 2023; Marciniak 2018).
   - Low amplitudes (< 0.2-0.3 mag) with 0.1-0.25 mag noise are where wrong unique solutions concentrate (Hanus & Durech 2012: 6 of 13 CSS-only unique models had periods different from the independent models).

results.claim: DAMIT/Asteroids@home uniqueness criterion chi2_tr = (1 + 0.5*sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min; replaced fixed 5% rule; empirical; 1/2 factor so threshold not too strict; old 5% corresponds to nu=200.
results.source: Durech, Hanus & Ali-Lagoa 2018, A&A 617, A57, arXiv:1807.02083
results.evidence: ar5iv text: threshold (1+0.5 sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min, 'nothing more than an empirical prescription to take into account the number of measurements'. The factor 1/2 is 'an adjustment without which the threshold would be too high'. The previous fixed 5% threshold (1.05 chi2_min) 'now corresponds to nu=200'. The threshold is used for periods. Pole solutions are also counted with chi2_tr: more than two poles means the model is reported as 'partial'.

results.claim: Parameter count: 3 spin + 3 phase-function + (n+1)^2 shape (convex) or 2 axis ratios (ellipsoid); periodograms with convex n=3, n=6 and ellipsoids; unique periods from n=3 and n=6 must agree.
results.source: Durech, Hanus & Ali-Lagoa 2018, A&A 617, A57, arXiv:1807.02083
results.evidence: The paper says 'three parameters for the spin state, three parameters to fit the photometric phase function, and (n+1)^2 shape parameters with convex shapes or two parameters for ellipsoids'. The 2-100 h interval was scanned 'independently with convex models with two shape resolutions n=3 and n=6 and with ellipsoids'. 'The unique periods for two different resolutions of the convex model had to be the same within the error interval.'

results.claim: Gaia DR2: chi2_tr = (1 + sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min; p=6 ellipsoids, p=20 convex n=3 (16 shape coeffs); periodograms with all RMS < 0.005 mag rejected as noise-fitting; only one period could have RMS < 0.01.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91, arXiv:1810.04485
results.corrected_claim: For DR2 the factor 1/2 was dropped: chi2_tr = (1 + sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min, described as an arbitrary trade-off borderline. p=6 for ellipsoids (P, lambda, beta, linear phase slope, a/c, b/c). p=20 for convex n=3, which is 16 shape parameters plus 4. The RMS rule is the reverse of what was claimed: 'To avoid fitting noise', only periodograms with ALL RMS values > 0.005 mag were kept. A periodogram was therefore excluded if ANY period had RMS <= 0.005; the reason given is that small-N data gave near-zero RMS for many periods. Only one period could have RMS < 0.01; otherwise the solution was non-unique.
results.evidence: PDF text (arXiv v1): 'now there is no factor of 1/2. This is an arbitrary borderline...'; '16 shape parameters, so the total number of parameters is p = 20'; 'To avoid fitting noise, we only selected periodograms with all RMS values > 0.005 mag. Another requirement was that there should be only one period with RMS below 0.01.'

results.claim: Lowell+Gaia DR2: k calibrated vs LCDB U>=3 (within 10%); convex w=0.01: k=1 287 (87%), k=1/2 522 (86%), k=1/3 641 (83%); ellipsoids k=1 710 (90%); w=0.01 from 0.1 vs 0.01 mag; adopted printed as k=3 convex, k=1 ellipsoids; ~15% wrong before further checks.
results.source: Durech, Hanus & Vanco 2019, A&A 631, A2, arXiv:1909.09395
results.evidence: In Table 1, the w=0.01 column for convex models reads k=1: 287 (87%), k=1/2: 522 (86%), k=1/3: 641 (83%). For ellipsoids with k=1 it reads 710 (90%). The text says 'we adopted values w=0.01, k=3 for convex models and k=1 for ellipsoids', so k=3 is printed. On the weight: if Lowell uncertainty is 0.1 mag and Gaia's is 0.01 mag, 'the weight of Lowell data with respect to Gaia should be w=0.01'. Other quotes: 'The fraction of incorrect periods is not negligible (~15%)'. A model counted as correct if its period was within 10% of an LCDB U>=3 period.

results.claim: Gaia DR3: chi2_tr=(1+sqrt(2/nu))chi2_min, RMS of every local minimum >0.01, min relative error 0.01, convex degree 3 with 15 optimized coefficients, inertia <1.1, mirror-pole check; false-solution rate 5/848.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24, arXiv:2305.10798
results.evidence: arXiv HTML: unique if all other periods give chi2 higher than '(1+sqrt(2/nu))chi2_min'. Also 'RMS residuals of all local minima had to be higher than 0.01' and 'minimum relative error to 0.01'. Shape: 'only the remaining 15 alm, blm parameters are optimized', with a0 fixed. Inertia ratio less than 1.1. Pole pairs with latitude difference >50 deg and longitude difference <120 deg were rejected. Out of 848 U=3 cases 'only five periods were incorrectly determined', which the paper calls about 0.6%.

results.claim: ASAS-SN: p chosen from false-solution rate vs LCDB flag-3; below p=0.5 false rate rises quickly; p=0.5 convex, p=0.6 ellipsoids; ~3% convex periods inconsistent with LCDB.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2021, A&A 654, A48, arXiv:2107.10027
results.evidence: 'For p<0.5, f_inc increases rather rapidly. So we select p=0.5 as an optimal value in the CI and p=0.6 in the tri-axial ellipsoid shape analyses.' 'about 3% of periods derived by CI from ASAS-SN data are inconsistent with the LCDB periods.' LCDB flags '3' and '3-' were used.

results.claim: Older AstDyS/MPC criterion: best period >=10% lower chi2 than all others; only one pole (up to lambda+-180) >=10% lower; reject if chi2 at 2P or P/2 below 1.1 chi2(P).
results.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134, arXiv:1104.4114
results.evidence: Sec 3.1: '(i) the best period has at least 10% lower chi2 than all other periods in the scanned interval, (ii) ... only one pole solution with at least 10% lower chi2 than the others (with a possible ambiguity for lambda+-180)'. Sec 3.3: 'if the chi2 was lower than 1.1 chi2 of the solution with period P, we rejected the model as unreliable'.

results.claim: Formal significance tests unusable due to systematics; Test 1 5% margin outside Pmin +- 0.5 Pmin^2/dT for ~1% false positives; n=3/n=6 agree; Pmin<20 h; <=2 poles >30 deg apart; inertia; bootstrap; visual.
results.source: Durech, Hanus, Oszkiewicz & Vanco 2016, A&A 587, A48, arXiv:1601.02909
results.evidence: 'We could not use formal statistical tools ... because the data were also affected by systematic errors.' Test 1: 5% lower outside 'P_min+-0.5P_min^2/DeltaT', where 5% was chosen 'while keeping the number of a false positive solution very low (~1%)'. The other tests are as listed: two resolutions must agree, P<20 h without an LCDB prior, at most two poles farther than 30 deg apart, the latitude/longitude condition, inertia <1.1, bootstrap, and a visual check.

results.claim: Bootstrap test Lowell: resampled same number of points, full period search rerun with convex or ellipsoids; kept only if bootstrap Pmin matched original.
results.source: Durech et al. 2016, A&A 587, A48, arXiv:1601.02909
results.evidence: The paper says 'randomly selecting the same number of observations from the original data set'. The new data set 'was processed the same way as the original one (using either convex shapes or ellipsoids for the period search)'. A model was 'stable only if the best-fit period Pmin from the bootstrapped data agreed with that from the original data'.

results.claim: Inertia ratio <1.1; two poles: |beta1-beta2|<50 deg and mod(|lambda1-lambda2|,180)>120 deg; unrealistically elongated/flat models rejected visually.
results.source: Durech et al. 2016, A&A 587, A48, arXiv:1601.02909
results.evidence: Quoted: inertia ratio 'should be less than 1.1'. 'the difference in ecliptic latitudes |b1-b2| has to be less than 50 deg and ... mod(|l1-l2|,180) has to be larger than 120 deg'. 'In some rare cases we rejected models that formally fitted the data, passed all the test, but were unrealistically elongated or flat.' Two parts of the claim are not in the source. These are tests of this paper's pipeline, not a rule for 'every convexinv result'. The link to the lambda+-180 ambiguity is the claimant's interpretation.

results.claim: ATLAS: 100 bootstrap resamples, with replacement, keeping number of points per filter; convexinv restarted from original spin; SDs of lambda, beta, P, c-o give errors.
results.source: Durech et al. 2020, A&A 643, A59, arXiv:2010.01820
results.evidence: 'We created one hundred bootstrapped data samples ... randomly sampled with a replacement; the number of data points observed in each filter remained the same.' Each sample was run 'using the spin parameters (lambda,beta,P) of the original model as initial values'. Uncertainties of lambda, beta, P and c-o are each the 'standard deviation of the sample for one hundred values'.

results.claim: Bootstrap convex inversion: 25 resamples, filters resampled independently, N_BS = matches within 1%; N_BS=25 ~99.5% correct; 885 of 904 agree with LCDB within 5%.
results.source: Durech, Vavra, Vanco & Erasmus 2022, Front. Astron. Space Sci. 9, 809771, DOI:10.3389/fspas.2022.809771
results.evidence: Publisher page: '25 bootstrapped samples of the original data set in both filters independently'. 'the same' means 'relative difference was not larger than 1%'. Table 1 gives 99.5% for N_BS=25. 'For 885 cases, the ATLAS period agrees with P_DB. However, 19 asteroids have different periods'. Agreement criterion: 'relative difference is less than 5%'.

results.claim: DR3 jackknife: 10 random parts, drop one (10%), repeat 10 times; keep if >=9 of 10 match within 0.1%; 20 asteroids with convex/ellipsoid disagreement excluded.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24, arXiv:2305.10798
results.evidence: Kept asteroids 'for which all ten jackknife periods were the same (within 0.1%) as the original period or for which there was at most one disagreement'. 'Among them we found 20 asteroids for which the periods were different; we excluded them.'

results.claim: DR2: removing 10% (2-5 points) usually left period unchanged; 44 cases same period but below threshold; 1 changed.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91, arXiv:1810.04485
results.evidence: The paper removed '10% of the data points (i.e. 2-5 points)'. 'In 44 cases, the reduced data set still provided the same best period, but it did not pass the threshold limit. In one case the new period was different.' Also: 'we are at the critical limit of the number of data points in many cases.' Note the wording: the reduced-data period did not pass the threshold. 'Fell below' in the claim means the same thing.
