results.claim: Sparse-only models: (a) 90% data rerun: 5 of 63 lost uniqueness, none switched; (b) ten mock shapes per model, most recovered, pole scatter ~+-10 deg.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134, arXiv:1104.4114
results.evidence: Data were reduced 'to 90%'. Losing uniqueness 'was true for five asteroids' out of the 63. 'we did not find two different but formally correct solutions when using the full versus reduced data sets.' 'a set of ten mock objects', 'unique models for most of their mock objects'. 'The typical uncertainty in pole direction was +-10 deg and, for the period, ~0.1 times the difference between the two local minimums.'

results.claim: 50 random poles per model, synthetic data + real relative residuals; sigma ~10 deg beta, ~5 deg/cos(beta) lambda; ~30% fewer successes for |beta|~0 than |beta|>53 deg; bias to high-latitude poles.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134, arXiv:1104.4114
results.evidence: Sec 4.3: 'we repeated steps 1-4 for 50 random poles for each asteroid model'. Noise came from relative residuals delta_i=(L_obs-L_mod)/L_mod. The standard deviations were (-0.2;10.2) for latitude and (-0.2;5.2) for longitude, i.e. '~5 deg/cos beta in lambda and ~10 deg in beta'. 'The amount of successfully derived models with |beta|~0 is about 30% lower than with |beta|>53 deg.'

results.claim: Catalina-only: correct models recovered at most resolutions n=2-6; wrong unique solutions mainly n=6 (sometimes 4-5), never n=2-3; recommend n=6 and Pstep=0.5dP then rerun n=3; accept only if similar.
results.source: Hanus & Durech 2012, Planet. Space Sci. 73, 75, arXiv:1301.7205
results.evidence: Correct models 'are mostly determined for other resolutions n and both period steps'. For incorrect models, 'unique solutions for different resolutions n and period steps Pstep only rarely and never for n=2 or n=3. All these unique solutions were always also incorrect.' The recommendation is to start with n=6, Pstep=0.5 DeltaP, then 'rerun with n=3 and Pstep=0.5DeltaP. The model is then reliable if we get similar unique solutions.' The claim's 'mainly n=6 (sometimes 4-5)' is a fair paraphrase; the source itself only says 'rarely'.

results.claim: Catalina-only, >=50 points, 185 asteroids with DAMIT models: 13 unique, only 7 agreed; causes: low amplitude, too few data for parameters, survey systematics; 'too perfect' RMS can flag but not reliably.
results.source: Hanus & Durech 2012, Planet. Space Sci. 73, 75, arXiv:1301.7205
results.evidence: 185 asteroids with >=50 CSS points gave 13 unique solutions. 'Only in 7 cases the solution was in an agreement with the model based on a different data set.' Three causes are listed: noisier data for low amplitudes, little data relative to the number of parameters, and survey systematics. 'Incorrectly determined models could be indicated by unrealistic rms values, but not generally.'

results.claim: MPC systematics (Oszkiewicz 2011): magnitude-dependent, saturation bright, background faint; most incorrect CSS-only models for brighter asteroids; CSS ~12%; useful mainly for amplitudes >=0.3 mag.
results.source: Hanus & Durech 2012, Planet. Space Sci. 73, 75, arXiv:1301.7205
results.corrected_claim: Confirmed: citing Oszkiewicz et al. 2011, errors depend on apparent magnitude, with saturation for the brightest and imperfect background subtraction for the faintest. CSS accuracy is ~12%, and the data are valuable for lightcurve amplitudes >~0.3 mag. Ambiguous: the paper says most incorrect models are 'brighter (have higher absolute magnitudes)' than the correct ones. That is self-contradictory, because a higher H means a fainter, smaller object. Whether the incorrect models are brighter or fainter is therefore ambiguous in the source, and the claim should not state 'brighter' without this caveat.
results.evidence: ar5iv: 'For the brightest asteroids, the images are saturated, and for the faintest, the background subtraction is imperfect.' 'Most of the incorrect models are brighter (have higher absolute magnitudes) than the correct ones.' 'valuable for asteroids with lightcurve amplitudes higher than >~0.3 mag'.

results.claim: AstDyS screening: magnitudes mostly 0.1 mag; phase function a*exp(-alpha/b)+c*alpha+d; Table 1 medians/weights (rel. to ~0.02 mag dense): 704 0.42 rejected, 691 0.24 rejected, 703 0.19 w=0.15, 699 0.18 w=0.1, G96 0.17 w=0.1, E12 0.15 w=0.1, 950 0.15 w=0.15, 689 0.15 w=0.3, Hipparcos 0.11 w=0.3.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2011, A&A 530, A134, arXiv:1104.4114
results.evidence: Magnitudes are 'given to only one decimal place, i.e., the accuracy is 0.1 mag at best'. Phase function f(alpha)=cos^2(alpha/2)[a exp(-alpha/b)+c alpha+d]. The cos^2 factor is omitted in the claim but the bracket matches. Dense lightcurve accuracy is ~0.02 mag (unit weight). Table 1 medians and weights: 704 0.42 (w=0); 691 0.24 (w=0); 703 0.19 (w=0.15); 699 0.18 (0.1); G96 0.17 (0.1); E12 0.15 (0.1); 950 0.15 (0.15); 689 0.15 (0.3); Hip 0.11 (0.3). Text: '(>~0.2 mag for both) are not suitable for the lightcurve inversion'.

results.claim: Review: noisy sparse/few points -> triaxial ellipsoid usually enough for period and pole, faster scan; survey data rarely better than 0.1 mag; many physically acceptable models fit to noise level.
results.source: Durech, Carry, Delbo, Kaasalainen & Viikinkoski 2015, Asteroids IV, arXiv:1502.04816
results.evidence: Text: 'When using noisy sparse data or only a limited number of data points, a simple shape model of a triaxial ellipsoid is usually sufficient...'. The shape is 'described by only two parameters (axes ratios)' and scanning is 'much faster'. 'Current surveys provide data of accuracy scarcely better than 0.1 mag.' 'many physically acceptable models fitting the data to the noise level.'

results.claim: Once a model fits to noise level, extra shape freedom does not improve fit; recommend several solutions with different model types and caution.
results.source: Durech et al. 2015, Asteroids IV, arXiv:1502.04816
results.evidence: 'Nonconvex models seldom fit lightcurves better than convex ones simply because the latter typically already fit the data down to noise level.' 'one should produce several solutions with various model types and parameters, and be very cautious about the results.'

results.claim: Ellipsoid scan: analytic brightness (~100x faster), rotation about max-inertia axis automatically; flexible convex can fit wrong period with nonphysical shape; ellipsoid best period then refined with convex for pole.
results.source: Durech, Hanus & Ali-Lagoa 2018, A&A 617, A57, arXiv:1807.02083
results.evidence: The paper says 'approximately one hundred times faster' because 'the brightness can be computed analytically'. Also 'the rotation is around the shortest axis with the maximum moment of inertia', and 'convex models can formally fit the data with an incorrect period with a nonphysical shape due to their flexibility'. 'After finding the best rotation period with the ellipsoidal model, we switched back to convex shape representation for the subsequent pole search.'

results.claim: Ellipsoids (Kaasalainen & Durech 2007) often give unique correct period; labels C/E/CE; (540) Rosamunde: ellipsoid best 7.82 h passed all tests but wrong; DAMIT 9.35 h only convex runner-up.
results.source: Durech et al. 2016, A&A 587, A48, arXiv:1601.02909
results.corrected_claim: Ellipsoid model (Kaasalainen & Durech 2007; geometric scattering) is 'sufficient to reveal the correct rotation period'; labels C, E, CE (both gave same unique period). Rosamunde caveat reversed: the convex periodogram's deepest minimum WAS the DAMIT period 9.34780 h, but it was not deep enough to pass test 1 (5% margin). The second-best convex minimum at 7.82166 h was the best ellipsoid solution, passed all tests and gave a wrong model.
results.evidence: ar5iv: 'the periodogram obtained with the convex model approach shows a minimum for 9.34780 h - the same as the DAMIT model ... this minimum was not deep enough to pass the test nr. 1. However, the second-best minimum for a convex model at 7.82166 h appeared as the best solution for the ellipsoid approach and passed all tests leading to a wrong model.'

results.claim: DR2 vs LCDB: convex produce false half periods, ellipsoids avoid; both unreliable for N<~30 (success >0.5 only for N>30); convex fits tend toward wrong shorter periods.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91, arXiv:1810.04485
results.corrected_claim: Convex models give false half-period solutions because they 'produce lightcurves with only one minimum/maximum per rotation'. Ellipsoids avoid this, but their periods from few points are often wrong. The fraction of correct periods (within +-5% of LCDB) rises above 0.5 when N>30; Fig. 2 shows both families, and convex models were run only for N>20. The tendency toward wrong shorter periods is not attributed to convex fits specifically. It is stated generally: 'the way the model is constructed' makes a shorter incorrect period easier to fit.
results.evidence: PDF text: 'The minor diagonal in the left panel are false solutions with the derived period being half of the real one; this can happen with convex shapes...'. 'The fraction of correctly determined periods (defined as those that agree with LCDB values within +-5%) increases above 0.5 when N > 30.' 'The clustering of points around shorter periods is likely a consequence of the way the model is constructed'. The Fig. 2 caption covers 'ellipsoidal and convex models'.

results.claim: Ellipsoid fails for non-double-sinusoid lightcurves; DR3 ellipsoid periodograms 16,010 unique; 5,784 ellipsoid-based and 6,269 convex-based survived jackknife; 3,431 both; 20 disagreeing discarded.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24, arXiv:2305.10798
results.evidence: 'ellipsoidal shape models are insufficient when an asteroid's light curve significantly differs from a simple double sinusoidal curve.' 'The analysis of ellipsoid-based periodograms resulted in 16,010 unique periods'. After jackknife there were '6269 models based on a convex-shape period search and 5784 models based on ... ellipsoids'. 3431 asteroids had both, and 20 with differing periods were excluded.

results.claim: Convex often fits P and P/2 equally; ellipsoids prefer true P; convex P/2 nonphysical (rotation about longest axis); ellipsoid only for period, shape from convex.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2021, A&A 654, A48, arXiv:2107.10027
results.evidence: Text: 'convex inversion often results in similarly good fits for both the correct period P and its multiples, most commonly P/2, light curve inversion with tri-axial ellipsoids usually favors only the correct period P'. P/2 solutions 'tend to force the principle rotation axis c to be the longest, which is nonphysical'. 'We only use the ellipsoidal model for the rotation period and then compute the shape using the convex inversion method.'

results.claim: MCMC inversion of Gaia DR3 with ellipsoids and convex shapes: for most objects ellipsoid poles match convex poles; 15% of convex shapes rejected (abstract only).
results.evidence: aanda.org returned 403 for us too. The Crossref API record (same DOI, A&A 707, A131, MacLennan, Pentikainen, Uvarova, Muinonen et al.) has the abstract. It says 'For the vast majority of our objects the best-fit ellipsoid spin poles are comparable to that of a convex shape' and 'We rejected 15% of convex shapes'. It also has the quoted sentence 'The assumption of ellipsoid shape for sparse datasets is sufficient for estimating the spin pole longitude and latitude.' We found no arXiv version; a search-suggested id, 2510.07524, is an unrelated paper.

results.claim: Simulated Gaia sparse photometry of complex shapes inverted with ellipsoids: recovered ellipsoids close to best-fitting ellipsoids; volume error ~10%.
results.source: Carbognani et al. 2012, Planet. Space Sci. 73, 80, arXiv:1903.12633, DOI:10.1016/j.pss.2011.12.002
results.evidence: arXiv abstract: 'the ellipsoids by photometry inversion are closely similar to the best-fitting ellipsoids of the simulated complex shapes' and 'the error on the asteroid volume (relative to a complex shape) is generally low, usually around 10%.' The journal ref is PSS 73, 80-85 (2012).

results.claim: Low-res sparse convex shapes not real; n=3 sharp edges, triangular pole-on; period/pole less sensitive to resolution; Durech 2016 found sparse shapes more angular with artificial sharp edges.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91, arXiv:1810.04485
results.evidence: PDF text: shapes were 'often unrealistic with sharp edges and triangular pole-on silhouettes', a consequence of n=3 being too low. 'convex shape models derived from DR2 data should not be taken as real shapes'. 'the rotation periods and pole directions are not that sensitive to the resolution and they are more reliable (Hanus & Durech 2012)'. 'Much less sensitive' is slightly stronger than 'not that sensitive'. The 2016 statement is verified directly in arXiv:1601.02909: shapes from sparse photometry 'are more angular ... and often have artificial sharp edges'. It is not cited in this DR2 passage.

results.claim: Lowell vs 279 DAMIT: 275 same period and pole diff <50 deg, mean 15, median 13 deg (DAMIT ~5-10 deg); 4 clearly different; false-positive few percent, DAMIT biased against low-amplitude long-period so real rate may be higher.
results.source: Durech et al. 2016, A&A 587, A48, arXiv:1601.02909
results.evidence: '279 models in DAMIT'; '275 models have the same rotation periods ... and the pole differences <50'. 'the mean value is 15 deg and the median 13 deg ... assuming that the poles from DAMIT have smaller errors (typically 5-10 deg)'. Four were discrepant. False positives are 'around a few percent', but the DAMIT sample 'is itself biased against low-amplitude long-period asteroids ... real number ... might be higher'.

results.claim: Lowell+WISE vs 246 DAMIT: 5 periods differ ~1e-4 (adjacent minima) with very different poles; 4 completely different; 237 matching mean 12 median 9 deg; axis ratios 1.06+-0.13 and 1.06+-0.18; sparse less elongated.
results.source: Durech, Hanus & Ali-Lagoa 2018, A&A 617, A57, arXiv:1807.02083
results.evidence: Of 246 models, five periods differed: 'corresponded to different local minima; the relative difference ... only 10^-4, but in most cases ... led to largely different pole directions'. 'Periods for four other asteroids were completely different.' The remaining 237 were correct, with mean pole difference 12 deg and median 9 deg. (a/b) ratio ~1.06 with SD 0.13; (b/c) mean 1.06 with SD 0.18. 'on average, our models are slightly less elongated than their counterparts in DAMIT.' Minor wording point: poles were very different 'in most cases', not in all five.

results.claim: DR2 vs 44 DAMIT: mean pole diff 20 deg, 7 outliers >60 deg; one DAMIT sparse-only wrong (wrong local minimum), 5 adjacent minima, 1 completely different period.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2018, A&A 620, A91, arXiv:1810.04485
results.evidence: PDF text: 'Most of our models agreed ... mean difference between their pole directions was 20 deg'. There were 'clear outliers with differences ... > 60 deg ... (seven in total)'. '(2802) Weisell - the DAMIT model based only on sparse data (Hanus et al. 2016) was clearly incorrect because the period search was done in the wrong local minimum.' 'In five cases ... a different local minimum leading to a different pole. In one case, the periods were completely different.'

results.claim: 33 DR3 periods differed from DAMIT; most DAMIT judged wrong; typically sparse-only, often Lowell; only 2 of 33 DR3 clearly wrong.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24, arXiv:2305.10798
results.evidence: 'For 33 asteroids, their DAMIT periods are different ... in most cases, our DR3 solutions are more reliable ... Only two of our 33 DR3 solutions are clearly wrong.' 'These incorrect DAMIT solutions are usually based on sparse data only, often on the Lowell Observatory dataset with poor photometric quality.'

results.claim: ASAS-SN vs DAMIT: pole differences rarely >30 deg; four inconsistent, two with twice the DAMIT period.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2021, A&A 654, A48, arXiv:2107.10027
results.evidence: 'The difference is rarely larger than 30 deg'. 'We identified four solutions that were inconsistent with those from DAMIT.' 'In two cases, we derived a rotation period that is twice that of DAMIT (asteroids 1461 and 16009).'

results.claim: Pole uncertainty by data type: <5 deg dense multi-apparition; 5-10 deg dense+sparse; 10-30 deg beta and 10-30/cos(beta) lambda few-app dense+sparse or sparse only; weights 0.3 (689), 0.15 (703), 0.1 Lowell.
results.evidence: The paper gives '<~5 deg in latitude beta and <~5 deg/cos beta in longitude' for rich dense data. Combined multi-apparition dense+sparse gets '~5-10 deg in beta and ~5-10 deg/cos beta in lambda'. Few-apparition dense+sparse or sparse-only gets '~10-30 deg in beta and ~10-30 deg/cos beta in lambda'. Weights relative to dense data: 689: 0.3, 703: 0.15, Lowell: 0.1.

results.claim: Catalina-only models: ~1e-4 to 1e-5 h period, 20-40 deg pole uncertainty; sparse-only shapes angular, sharp edges, planar areas; >~10 dense LCs from >~2 apparitions smooth them, better fit to occultations.
results.source: Hanus et al. 2013, A&A 551, A67, arXiv:1301.6943
results.evidence: 'We also derived 20 asteroid models based purely on sparse-in-time photometry from the Catalina Sky Survey', with 'typical uncertainty of the sidereal rotational period is ~10^-4-10^-5 h and of the pole direction 20-40 deg'. Shapes 'tend to be very angular, with sharp edges and large planar areas'. 'A substantial addition (>~10 lightcurves from >~2 apparitions) of dense lightcurves smooths the shape models out ... better fit to occultation chords'.

results.claim: Occultations often reject one of two mirror poles; sizes ~10%.
results.evidence: Abstract: 'In many cases, occultations allow us to reject one of two possible pole solutions that were derived from photometry.' 'we can determine the asteroid size with a relative accuracy of typically ~10%.'

results.claim: sHG1G2 on ZTF: 6,499 objects vs literature (mostly DAMIT): separation peaks ~20 deg, half within 35 deg; ~60% within 1 sigma, 95% within 3 sigma, realistic uncertainties.
results.evidence: arXiv PDF text: 'We find 6,499 SSOs with previous estimates of the spin-axis coordinates, mainly from the lightcurve inversion technique ... compiled on the DAMIT service'. 'The distribution peaks around 20 deg, with half of the SSOs agreeing below 35 deg.' 'About 60% of the solutions agree within one sigma, and 95% at three sigma, an indication that uncertainties seems properly estimated'.

results.claim: sHG1G2 often not needed: near-spherical, obliquity ~0/180, narrow aspect range -> fits no better than HG1G2; recommend fitting 'from the most robust to the most informative', fallback to simpler.
results.source: Carry et al. 2024, A&A 687, A38, arXiv:2403.20179
results.evidence: PDF text: 'This implies that the predictions by HG or HG1G2 fit equally well the data as sHG1G2, although the latter has more degrees of freedom. There are three cases in which sHG1G2 may not be required': (nearly) spherical, obliquity close to 0 or 180 deg, and limited aspect-angle range. 'HG, HG1G2, and sHG1G2 models should be computed for each SSO ...: from the most robust to the most informative. In the pathological cases ... HG1G2 should then be preferred'.

results.claim: Cibulkova 2016: geometric-scattering ellipsoids fit to per-apparition mean brightness and dispersion (Lowell); synthetic DAMIT+Hapke test: lambda reliable, beta biased; model noise 0.06; noise larger for fainter (0.08 best for bright DAMIT).
results.source: Cibulkova, Durech, Vokrouhlicky, Kaasalainen & Oszkiewicz 2016, A&A 596, A57, arXiv:1610.02790
results.evidence: The paper uses 'geometrically scattering triaxial ellipsoids', comparing mean brightness and brightness dispersion per apparition. Synthetic data were made with DAMIT shapes and Hapke scattering. '(i) determination of lambda is reliable in a statistical sense, while (ii) determination of beta is subject to systematic bias'. sigma_model = 0.06 covers the Hapke and ellipsoid assumptions. 'less bright asteroids have higher noise level'; sigma_L = 0.08 worked best for the preferentially brighter DAMIT asteroids.

results.claim: Bowell 2014: >350,000 spin longitudes from mean brightness vs ecliptic longitude (sin 2lambda); reliable for p-p >0.15 mag and >=~50 obs; first harmonic overfits for 1.7%; MPC mixed sources with time-variable errors.
results.source: Bowell et al. 2014, Meteorit. Planet. Sci. 49, 95, arXiv:1310.3617
results.evidence: arXiv PDF text: 'spin-axis longitudes for more than 350 000 asteroids'. 'For the remaining 1.7% of the objects, the fit including both harmonics over-fits the noisy data.' 'significant peak-to-peak brightness variation (> 0.15 mag)'. 'asteroids having small numbers of observations (fewer than 50, say) cannot usually be reliably fitted'. 'low precision (generally rounded to 0.1 mag) and low accuracy (rms ... 0.2 to 0.3 mag are typical)'. 'each having different systematic and random errors, sometimes time variable'.

results.claim: Veres 2015: MPC problems: non-standard filters/no calibration; no colour transform to V; no per-obs uncertainties (back-calculated per observatory); 0.1 mag storage; default G; rotation amplitude ignored; MPC observatory-dependent corrections for Juric ~0.4 mag error.
results.source: Veres et al. 2015, Icarus 261, 34, arXiv:1506.00762
results.evidence: The paper lists: 'non-standard filters and/or without accurate calibration' and not performing 'the color transformation ... to the Johnson V-band'. Uncertainty 'must be statistically back-calculated for each observatory'. 'storing photometric values with only 0.1 mags precision'. 'Assuming that G_B=0.15'. 'lack of information about their rotation amplitudes induces an error'. 'Juric et al. 2002 first reported a systematic error of about 0.4 mags ... which the MPC (and others) now attempt to address with observatory-dependent corrections'.

results.claim: Pravec 2012: catalog H for H>10-12 too bright, 0.4-0.5 mag near H=14; suspected survey magnitudes; clear/no-filter w/o code taken as B; R reported as V off 0.4-0.5; default G=0.15 and V-R=0.40 taxonomy-dependent offsets.
results.source: Pravec et al. 2012, Icarus 221, 365 (author PDF)
results.evidence: Author PDF text: the offset 'becomes prominent in a range of H greater than 10 and is particularly big above H ~ 12', 'catalog H values are systematically too bright', and 'reaches a maximum around H = 14 where the mean (Hcatalog - H) is -0.4 to -0.5'. Also 'we suspect that the problem lies in the magnitude estimates reported by asteroid surveys'. 'if observations taken with a clear or no filter are reported without a filter code, the magnitude estimates are taken as B band'. R reported as V are 'off by about 0.4 or 0.5 mag'. The default G of 0.15 and single (V-R)=0.40 offset S and C types in opposite directions. The paper presents these mechanisms as guesses and speculation.

results.claim: DePhOCUS: ~500,000 MPC obs; 703/G96 bias dropped >0.3/>0.1 mag summer 2018 (Gaia DR1->DR2); G96 rises after 2022 uncorrected; most V-band reporters, including 703/G96 with UCAC catalogs, ~+0.25 mag bias.
results.source: Hoffmann et al. 2024 (DePhOCUS), Icarus, arXiv:2408.07474
results.corrected_claim: The study analysed nearly 500,000 MPC observations of 468 asteroids. For 703 and G96 the bias dropped by more than 0.3 and 0.1 mag respectively in summer 2018, matching the switch from Gaia DR1 to DR2. The G96 increase after summer 2022 is not included in the corrections. Most major V-band reporters, 'among which' 703 and G96 (CSS), have a positive bias of ~0.25 mag. With the bias defined as predicted minus observed, positive means reported too bright. The source does not say 703/G96 used UCAC catalogs. Its UCAC numbers are per catalog: UCAC-2 +0.25 mag and UCAC-4 +0.12 mag, each ~20,000 observations.
results.evidence: arXiv HTML: 'the bias drops by more than 0.3/0.1 mag respectively'. 'This drop perfectly corresponds to the switch from Gaia DR1 to DR2 as reference star catalog'. 'most major observatories reporting in the V-band have a positive bias of around 0.25 mag, among which there are the telescopes with codes 703 and G96 from the CSS'. 'UCAC-2 and UCAC-4 catalog, each having around 20 000 observations, with +0.25 and +0.12 mag'.

results.claim: 704 (USNO-A): ~0 mag upper galactic hemisphere, ~-0.5 lower (separate N/S calibrations); grows with apparent magnitude; not constant before 2006; sky-position offsets can mimic aspect changes.
results.source: Hoffmann et al. 2024 (DePhOCUS), Icarus, arXiv:2408.07474
results.evidence: Station 704 used USNO-A1.0/A2.0. 'the upper hemisphere has a bias around 0 mag, while the lower hemisphere has a bias around -0.5 mag', attributed to 'separate calibrations for the northern and southern sky'. Also 'increase of bias with increasing apparent magnitude'. Time trend: 'steep increase ... up to the year 2000 and the consequent shallow decrease up to the year 2006'. The last sentence, that offsets can masquerade as aspect changes, is the claimant's own inference and is not stated in the source.

results.claim: Seven largest stations; T05/T08 stable but >19 mag biased bright (selection); F51 fast movers too faint; C57 no photometric deviation despite astrometric errors; 0.10 mag precision + no LC correction -> ~0.25 mag RMS floor.
results.source: Hoffmann et al. 2024 (DePhOCUS), Icarus, arXiv:2408.07474
results.evidence: The paper lists the stations as C57, 703, T08, T05, 704, G96 and F51. For T05/T08: 'no change of bias visible over time'. Above magnitude 19 'there is an increase of bias ... reported brighter than they should be', explained by selection toward amplitude maxima near the limiting magnitude. 'Code F51 ... has the tendency to have an increasingly negative bias for high motions'; with bias defined as predicted minus observed, negative means too faint. For C57: 'despite having significant errors in the astrometry, does not seem to have systematic deviations'. 'Including the typical numerical precision ... of 0.10 mag, a minimum RMS of roughly 0.25 mag is expected as a physical boundary'.

results.claim: Athanasopoulos 2022: CSS/USNO/ZTF from AstDyS plus ATLAS, ASAS-SN, Gaia, TESS; each survey+filter separately calibrated, normalized; sigma-clip; weight by expected RMS; one shared phase function (approximation); chi2_tr k=0.5; dP/P=P/(2T); period uncertainty ~dP/20.
results.source: Athanasopoulos et al. 2022, A&A, arXiv:2210.02096
results.evidence: 'The CSS, USNO-Flagstaff, and ZTF data were obtained through the AstDys-2 database'. The data set also includes ATLAS, ASAS-SN, Gaia DR2, PTF and TESS. 'each sparse dataset (i.e. specific survey and photometric filter) are internally calibrated'. Sigma-clipping is used, and datasets are weighted 'based on their accuracy (expected rms)'. A single phase function is used, with the caveat 'This is not fully correct'. The threshold is (1+0.5 sqrt(2/nu)) chi2_min, with DeltaP/P = 1/2 P/T. '~1/20 DeltaP is a reliable uncertainty ... rotation phase offset of about 10 deg'. The Gaia data were DR2.

results.claim: Oersted (~20 km) convexinv on MPC/AstDyS sparse data (CSS, ATLAS c/o, ASAS-SN, Gaia DR3, ZTF g/r, Pan-STARRS); well-defined global minimum below chi2 threshold gave single pole; checked vs multi-chord occultation.
results.source: Hanus, Delbo, Pokorny, Marchis & Esposito 2025, arXiv:2510.05843
results.corrected_claim: Confirmed: (16583) Oersted is ~20 km. Convex inversion was run on sparse data from CSS, ATLAS (c,o), ASAS-SN, Gaia DR3, ZTF (g,r) and Pan-STARRS, retrieved from the MPC and AstDyS. The periodogram shows a well-defined global minimum at P_sid ~ 4.9567 h. Only a single pole was found, which the authors attribute to the high orbital inclination. The model was scaled and checked against a multi-chord occultation and refined with ADAM. Not found in what we read: an explicit statement that the minimum was 'below the chi2 threshold'. Now published as A&A 704, A67 (2025).
results.evidence: arXiv HTML: 'The photometric points were retrieved from the Minor Planet Center and the AstDyS databases, and span multiple apparition epochs'. 'The global minimum, corresponding to a sidereal rotation period of Psid=4.956677 hours'. 'only a single pole solution was identified in this case'. 'The projected silhouette matches the occultation profile within the chord timing uncertainties'.

results.claim: ATLAS 2020: ~15% outliers beyond 2.5 RMS from phase fit; c-o free scale factor; separate slopes marginal; one-day cadence aliasing near 12/24/48 h; convex and ellipsoid scans (C/E/CE); ~5,000 of ~100,000 reliable.
results.source: Durech et al. 2020, A&A 643, A59, arXiv:2010.01820
results.evidence: Points beyond a '2.5 rms' limit from the fitted phase function were removed, which 'removed about 15% of the data points'. Color c-o 'was modeled as a free scale factor ... or equivalently as an offset in magnitude scale'. 'splitting photometry into two colors and fitting them with different slopes improves the fit, but usually not very significantly.' 'incorrectly resolving periods close to 12, 24, or 48 hours is a common problem with ATLAS data due to the one-day cadence'. Table A.1 notes 'C - convex models, E - ellipsoids, CE - both methods gave the same unique period'. 'almost a hundred thousand ... only about five thousand.'

results.claim: Westerwald (amplitude 0.12 mag): no unique convexinv solution until errors >0.2 mag removed; pole only 'retrograde'; spin errors from 1,000 bootstraps resampling c and o separately; ~10 yr ATLAS.
results.source: Erasmus, Durech et al. 2026, arXiv:2609.07404
results.evidence: arXiv HTML: 'The folded amplitude is low (0.12 mag; a/b>~1.11)'. 'removing points with errors larger than 0.2 mag and repeating the period search, we found the sideral rotation period P=3.636862'. 'many models with this rotation period but with different spin-axis orientations ... The only constraint ... the rotation is retrograde.' The bootstrap is the paper's general method: 'one thousand bootstrap data sets for each asteroid' with c and o resampled separately. Westerwald itself got no full model. The baseline is about a decade (MJD 57313-61034).

results.claim: Marciniak 2018: survey photometry 0.1-0.2 mag misses low-amplitude population; Petropolitana dense P=169.52 h vs 37.347 h sparse DAMIT (Hanus 2016, scan to 100 h).
results.source: Marciniak et al. 2018, A&A 610, A7, arXiv:1711.01893
results.evidence: ar5iv: 'very low photometric accuracy (0.1 - 0.2 mag on average, Hanus et al. 2011), so the modelling is missing most of the low-amplitude population'. Petropolitana dense-data period 169.52 +- 0.06 h, versus the Hanus et al. 2016 sparse model of 37.347 h from 'scanning a standard period span of up to 100 hours'.

results.claim: Santana-Ros 2015: 10,000 Gaia-like sparse datasets, ellipsoid genetic algorithm; biases for quasi-spherical and low pole latitudes (amplitude ~ noise); one dense LC reduces wrong solutions for N<50.
results.source: Santana-Ros et al. 2015, MNRAS, arXiv:1504.02809
results.evidence: The paper says 'The Gaia inversion algorithm is assuming the asteroids to have the shapes of triaxial ellipsoids'. The abstract says about 10,000 asteroids; the text gives 10,359. 'the results are biased for asteroids having quasi-spherical shapes and low pole latitudes', because the signal can be 'lost in the photometric random noise'. Adding a dense lightcurve makes it 'possible to reduce the number of wrong solutions for asteroids having less than 50 data points'.

results.claim: Muinonen 2020: Bayesian MCMC over convex shapes/spins, random+systematic errors, prior weights; separate uncertainty model for ellipsoid inversion; Lutetia vs Rosetta; no AIC/BIC in abstract.
results.source: Muinonen, Torppa, Wang, Cellino & Penttila 2020, A&A 642, A138, DOI:10.1051/0004-6361/202038036
results.evidence: Crossref abstract: 'We consider both random and systematic uncertainties (errors) in the observations, and assign weights ... Bayesian a priori probability densities.' They use an MCMC sampler for convex shapes. 'For inverse methods involving triaxial ellipsoids, we update the uncertainty model'. Lutetia results agree 'with those derived with the help of Rosetta'. There is no AIC/BIC. Calling it an 'alternative to fixed chi2 thresholds' is the claimant's framing.

results.claim: Waszczak 2015: period-quality classifier trained/cross-validated on 805 asteroids; 4% contamination from asteroids fitted independently in more than one opposition; no paper predicts withheld lightcurves.
results.source: Waszczak et al. 2015, AJ 150, 75, arXiv:1504.04041
results.corrected_claim: The classifier was trained and cross-validated on 927 lightcurves of 805 unique asteroids with LCDB U=3 periods: 1,000 trials, each with an 80/20 train/test split. The 4% contamination (~30/1413) comes from 654 asteroids with more than one reliable PTF fit (1,413 fits). These were observed 'in multiple oppositions and/or in both filters during one or more oppositions', not strictly in more than one opposition. The sentence 'No paper we read checks a model by predicting withheld lightcurves' is the claimant's own statement and cannot be checked against this source.
results.evidence: ar5iv: '927 lightcurves (805 unique asteroids) having a quality code 3 period'. '654 unique asteroids have more than one PTF lightcurve ... 1,413 fits ... observed in multiple oppositions and/or in both filters'. 'contamination fraction ... ~30/1413 = 4%'.

results.claim: Viikinkoski 2017: two shape parameterizations (octantoids, subdivision), only common features supported; jackknife leave-one-image-out.
results.source: Viikinkoski, Hanus, Kaasalainen, Marchis & Durech 2017, A&A, arXiv:1708.05191
results.evidence: ar5iv: 'The usage of different shape representations allows us to separate the effects of parametrization from the actual features supported by the data.' The two shape representations are octantoids and sqrt3-subdivision surfaces. Jackknife: n extra models, each leaving out one of the n AO images. For single-image targets, variability across parameterizations was used instead.

results.claim: Gaia ~0.01 mag needs tens of points, ground sparse hundreds; few-point shapes sensitive to N and resolution; only a/b of dynamically equivalent ellipsoid stable.
results.source: Durech & Hanus 2023, A&A 675, A24, arXiv:2305.10798
results.evidence: 'With Gaia, we need tens of data points, while with less accurate photometry we would need hundreds of them'. 'With only tens of observations the reconstructed shape model is sensitive to the number of observations, their distribution in time, and the model parameterization.' 'we utilize only the elongation a/b ... axis ratio of the dynamically equivalent ellipsoid. It is the primary and most stable parameter of the shape.'

results.claim: DAMIT software page: v0.2.1, C translation by Durech of Kaasalainen's Fortran, brief manuals and examples; convexinv (all params, spherical harmonics), conjgradinv (facet areas, polishing), lcgenerator; period_scan not named.
results.source: DAMIT software download page, https://damit.cuni.cz/projects/damit/pages/software_download (accessed 2026-10-05)
results.evidence: Page: version 0.2.1, 'developed by Mikko Kaasalainen in Fortran and converted to C by Josef Durech'. convexinv 'optimizes all parameters and uses spherical harmonics functions for shape representation'. conjgradinv 'optimizes only shape and uses directly facet areas ... for polishing'. lcgenerator computes synthetic lightcurves. The package includes 'brief manuals, example lightcurves'. Licence CC BY 4.0, tar.gz ~325 KiB. Our read of the page summary did not mention period_scan.
